statement: Wyznaczyć wszystkie dodatnie liczby całkowite $b$ o następującej własności: istnieją takie dodatnie liczby całkowite $a, k, \ell$, że liczby $a^{k}+b^{\ell}$ i $a^{\ell}+b^{k}$ są podzielne przez $b^{k+\ell}$, a przy tym $k \neq \ell$.
solution:
Sposób 1. Bez straty ogólności przyjmijmy, że $k>\ell$. Z założeń wynika, że liczba
$$
a^{k}+b^{\ell}-a^{k-\ell}\left(a^{\ell}+b^{k}\right)=b^{\ell}-a^{k-\ell} b^{k}
$$
dzieli się przez $b^{k+\ell}$. Zatem liczba $1-a^{k-\ell} b^{k-\ell}$ dzieli się przez $b^{k}$. W szczególności dzieli się przez $b$. W takim razie liczba
$$
1-a^{k-\ell} b^{k-\ell}+b \cdot a^{k-\ell} b^{k-\ell-1}=1
$$
dzieli się przez $b$. Stąd $b=1$.


Sposób 2. Bez straty ogólności załóżmy, że $k>\ell$. Z założeń wynika w szczególności, że $a^{\ell}+b^{k}$ dzieli się przez $b^{k}$, więc przez $b^{k}$ dzieli się też $a^{\ell}$. Ponieważ $k>\ell$, więc $a^{\ell}$ dzieli się przez $b^{\ell}$. Stąd $a$ dzieli się przez $b$. Wobec tego $a^{k}$ dzieli się przez $b^{k}$, ale z założeń zadania wynika też, że $a^{k}+b^{\ell}$ dzieli się przez $b^{k}$. W takim razie $b^{k}$ dzieli $b^{\ell}$. Jest to możliwe tylko gdy $b=1$, bo w przeciwnym razie $b^{k}>b^{\ell}$, a dzielnik danej liczby nie może być od niej większy.


Sposób 3. Rozważmy dowolną liczbę pierwszą $p$. Załóżmy, że $p$ wchodzi do rozkładu na liczby pierwsze liczb $a$ i $b$ odpowiednio z wykładnikami $x$ i $y$. Udowodnimy, że $y=0$. Załóżmy nie wprost, że $y \geqslant 1$. Z podzielności liczby $a^{k}+b^{\ell}$ przez $b^{k+\ell}$ wynika w szczególności, że dzieli się ona przez $p^{y \ell}$. Liczba $b^{\ell}$ też się przez nią dzieli, więc $a^{k}=\left(a^{k}+b^{\ell}\right)-b^{\ell}$ również.
Z drugiej strony, $a^{k}+b^{\ell}$ dzieli się przez $p^{y \ell+1}$, a $b^{\ell}$ nie. W takim razie liczba $a^{k}=\left(a^{k}+b^{\ell}\right)-b^{\ell}$ nie dzieli się przez $p^{y \ell+1}$. Wnioskujemy, że $p$ wchodzi do rozkładu na czynniki pierwsze liczby $a^{k}$ z wykładnikiem $y \ell$. Stąd $x k=y \ell$. Prowadząc analogiczne rozumowanie dla liczby $a^{\ell}+b^{k}$ dowodzimy, że $x \ell=y k$. Z otrzymanych równości wynika, że $k=\ell$ wbrew założeniom zadania. Założenie, że $y \geqslant 1$ doprowadziło do sprzeczności. W takim razie $y=0$ i liczba $b$ nie dzieli się przez $p$. Wobec dowolności wyboru $p$ oznacza to, że $b$ nie ma dzielników pierwszych. Stąd $b=1$.

statement:
Dla dowolnej liczby rzeczywistej $a$ i dowolnego $b>0$ rozszerzeniem przedziału domkniętego $[a-b, a+b] \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ nazwiemy przedział domknięty $[a-2b, a+2b]$. Powiemy, że przedziały $P_{1}, P_{2}, \ldots, P_{k}$ pokrywają zbiór $X$, jeśli $X \subseteq P_{1} \cup P_{2} \cup \ldots \cup P_{k}$.
Udowodnić, że istnieje liczba całkowita $M$ o następującej własności: dla dowolnego skończonego podzbioru $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ istnieje taki podzbiór $B \subseteq A$ składający się z co najwyżej $M$ liczb, że dla dowolnych stu przedziałów pokrywających zbiór $B$ ich rozszerzenia pokrywają zbiór $A$.
solution:
Udowodnimy przez indukcję ze względu na $k=1,2,3, \ldots$ następujące zdanie:
$\Phi(k)$ : Dla dowolnego niepustego skończonego podzbioru $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ istnieje taki podzbiór $B \subseteq A$ zawierający $\min A$ i $\max A$ i składający się z co najwyżej $2 \cdot 3^{k-1}$ liczb, że dla dowolnych $k$ przedziałów pokrywających zbiór $B$ ich rozszerzenia pokrywają zbiór $A$.
Jeśli $A$ jest zbiorem jednoelementowym, to zbiór $B=A$ spełnia żądane warunki. Od teraz zakładamy, że $A$ ma co najmniej dwa elementy.
Dla $k=1$ przyjmujemy $B=\{\min A, \max A\}$. Wówczas dowolny przedział pokrywający $B$ pokrywa także $A$, a więc jego rozszerzenie tym bardziej pokrywa $A$.
Załóżmy teraz, że zdanie $\Phi(k)$ jest prawdziwe dla pewnego $k \geqslant 1$. Udowodnimy zdanie $\Phi(k+1)$. Rozważmy dowolny skończony podzbiór $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ o co najmniej dwóch elementach. Niech $x=\min A$ i $y=\max A$. Podzielmy przedział $[x, y]$ na trzy części:
$$
P_{1}=\left[x, \frac{2x+y}{3}\right], \quad P_{2}=\left[\frac{2x+y}{3}, \frac{x+2y}{3}\right], \quad P_{3}=\left[\frac{x+2y}{3}, y\right] .
$$
Oznaczmy $A_{1}=A \cap P_{1}$, $A_{2}=A \cap P_{2}$ i $A_{3}=A \cap P_{3}$. Ze zdania $\Phi(k)$ wynika, że dla $i=1,2,3$ istnieje taki zbiór $B_{i} \subseteq A_{i}$ mający co najwyżej $2 \cdot 3^{k-1}$ elementów, że jeśli $k$ przedziałów pokrywa zbiór $B_{i}$, to ich rozszerzenia pokrywają zbiór $A_{i}$, a ponadto $x \in B_{1}$ i $y \in B_{3}$. Oznaczmy $B=B_{1} \cup B_{2} \cup B_{3}$. Wówczas $B$ ma co najwyżej $2 \cdot 3^{k}$ elementów i zawiera $x$ i $y$. Udowodnimy, że jeśli $k+1$ przedziałów pokrywa zbiór $B$, to ich rozszerzenia pokrywają zbiór $A$.
Rozważmy dowolne $k+1$ przedziałów $Q_{1}, Q_{2}, \ldots, Q_{k+1}$ pokrywających zbiór $B$. Jeżeli dla każdego $i=1,2,3$ zbiór $B_{i}$ jest pokryty przez nie więcej niż $k$ przedziałów spośród $Q_{1}, Q_{2}, \ldots, Q_{k+1}$, to ich rozszerzenia pokrywają zbiór $A_{i}$; w konsekwencji zbiór $A$ jest pokryty przez rozszerzenia $Q_{1}, Q_{2}, \ldots, Q_{k+1}$.
W przeciwnym razie któryś ze zbiorów $B_{1}, B_{2}, B_{3}$ niepusto przecina się z każdym z przedziałów $Q_{1}, Q_{2}, \ldots, Q_{k+1}$. Jeśli $B_{1}$ jest takim zbiorem, to rozważmy przedział $Q_{i}$, który zawiera $y$. Ze względu na to, że $Q_{i}$ zawiera jakiś element zbioru $B_{1}$, przedział $Q_{j}$ zawiera przedział $P_{2} \cup P_{3}$. Stąd jego rozszerzenie pokrywa przedział $[x, y]$ i w szczególności pokrywa zbiór $A$. Analogicznie dowodzimy, że jeśli $B_{3}$ niepusto przecina się z każdym z przedziałów $Q_{1}, Q_{2}, \ldots, Q_{k+1}$, to przedział $Q_{j}$ zawierający $x$ pokrywa $P_{1} \cup P_{2}$, więc jego rozszerzenie pokrywa $[x, y]$ i w szczególności pokrywa $A$.
Pozostał przypadek, w którym $B_{2}$ przecina się niepusto z każdym z przedziałów $Q_{1}, Q_{2}, \ldots, Q_{k+1}$. Rozważmy przedział $Q_{i}$ zawierający $y$ oraz przedział $Q_{j}$ zawierający $x$. Wówczas $Q_{i}$ pokrywa przedział $P_{3}$, a przedział $Q_{j}$ pokrywa przedział $P_{1}$. Ich rozszerzenia pokrywają odpowiednio przedziały $\left[\frac{x+y}{2}, y\right]$ oraz $\left[x, \frac{x+y}{2}\right]$. Stąd rozszerzenia przedziałów $Q_{i}$ i $Q_{j}$ pokrywają $[x, y]$ i w konsekwencji pokrywają $A$. To dowodzi prawdziwości zdania $\Phi(k+1)$.

Na mocy zasady indukcji matematycznej zdanie $\Phi(k)$ jest prawdziwe dla dowolnego $k \geqslant 1$. Ze zdania $\Phi(100)$ wynika, że liczba $M=2 \cdot 3^{99}$ spełnia warunki zadania.

statement: Dany jest taki ciąg liczb całkowitych $a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3}, \ldots$, że dla dowolnych dodatnich liczb całkowitych $k, \ell$ liczba $a_{k}+a_{\ell}$ dzieli się przez $k+\ell$. Udowodnić, że dla dowolnych dodatnich liczb całkowitych $k>\ell$ liczba $a_{k}-a_{\ell}$ dzieli się przez $k-\ell$.
solution:
Ustalmy dowolne dodatnie liczby całkowite $k>\ell$. Zauważmy, że dla dowolnego $m$ zachodzi równość
$$
a_{k}-a_{\ell}=\left(a_{k}+a_{m}\right)-\left(a_{m}+a_{\ell}\right) .
$$
Wystarczy dobrać liczbę $m$ w taki sposób, by liczby $a_{k}+a_{m}$ i $a_{m}+a_{\ell}$ były podzielne przez $k-\ell$. Z założeń zadania wynika, że liczba $a_{k}+a_{m}$ dzieli się przez $k+m$, a liczba $a_{m}+a_{\ell}$ dzieli się przez $m+\ell$. Wystarczy więc dobrać liczbę $m$ tak, aby liczby $k+m$ i $m+\ell$ były podzielne przez $k-\ell$. Połóżmy $m=(k+1)(k-\ell)-k$. Wówczas $m>0, k+m=(k+1)(k-\ell)$ oraz $m+\ell=k(k-\ell)$. Tak dobrana liczba $m$ spełnia więc omówione wyżej warunki dające tezę zadania.

statement:
Dana jest liczba pierwsza $p>2023$. Dla dowolnej liczby całkowitej $x$ symbolem $r(x)$ oznaczymy resztę z dzielenia liczby $x$ przez $p$. Niech $p_{1}<p_{2}<p_{3}<\ldots<p_{m}$ będą wszystkimi liczbami pierwszymi mniejszymi od $\sqrt[4]{\frac{1}{2} p}$. Załóżmy, że $q_{1}, q_{2}, \ldots, q_{m}$ są takimi liczbami całkowitymi, że liczby $p_{1} q_{1}-1, p_{2} q_{2}-1, \ldots, p_{m} q_{m}-1$ są podzielne przez $p$. Udowodnić, że dla dowolnych liczb całkowitych $0<a, b<p$ zbiory
$$
\left\{r\left(q_{1}\right), r\left(q_{2}\right), \ldots, r\left(q_{m}\right)\right\}, \quad\left\{r\left(a q_{1}+b\right), r\left(a q_{2}+b\right), \ldots, r\left(a q_{m}+b\right)\right\}
$$
mają co najwyżej trzy wspólne elementy.
solution:
Zauważmy, że liczby $r\left(q_{1}\right), r\left(q_{2}\right), \ldots, r\left(q_{m}\right)$ są parami różne. Rzeczywiście, jeśli $r\left(q_{i}\right)=r\left(q_{j}\right)$, to $q_{i} \equiv q_{j}(\bmod p)$. Po pomnożeniu przez $p_{i} p_{j}$ i skorzystaniu z tego, że $p_{i} q_{i} \equiv 1 \equiv p_{j} q_{j}(\bmod p)$ dostajemy $p_{i} \equiv p_{j} (\bmod p)$. To jednak oznacza, że $p_{i}=p_{j}$, bo $0<p_{i}, p_{j}<p$, skąd $i=j$.

Podobnie, liczby $r\left(a q_{1}+b\right), r\left(a q_{2}+b\right), \ldots, r\left(a q_{m}+b\right)$ są parami różne: jeśli $r\left(a q_{i}+b\right)=r\left(a q_{j}+b\right)$, to $a q_{i}+b \equiv a q_{j}+b(\bmod p)$, $a\left(q_{i}-q_{j}\right) \equiv 0 (\bmod p)$ i skoro $0<a<p$, to $q_{i}-q_{j} \equiv 0(\bmod p)$ i $r\left(q_{i}\right)=r\left(q_{j}\right)$.

Zauważmy, że $r\left(q_{i}\right)=r\left(a q_{i}+b\right)$ dla co najwyżej jednego indeksu $i$. Rzeczywiście, to jest równoważne kongruencji $q_{i} \equiv a q_{i}+b(\bmod p)$. Jeśli $a=1$, to takie $i$ w ogóle nie istnieje, bo wymuszałoby to $b \equiv 0(\bmod p)$, a jeśli $1<a<p$, to dana kongruencja jest równoważna $q_{i} \equiv b c(\bmod p)$, gdzie $c$ jest taką liczbą, że $(1-a) c \equiv 1(\bmod p)$. To jest równoważne $r\left(q_{i}\right)=r(b c)$, co oznacza, że potencjalny indeks $i$, który mógłby spełniać tę równość jest wyznaczony jednoznacznie.

Załóżmy nie wprost, że zbiory z zadania mają co najmniej cztery wspólne elementy. Wówczas dla pewnych parami różnych $i_{1}, i_{2}, i_{3}, i_{4}$ oraz pewnych $j_{1}, j_{2}, j_{3}, j_{4}$ mamy $r\left(q_{i_{k}}\right)=r\left(a q_{j_{k}}+b\right)$ dla $k=1,2,3,4$. Wówczas również $j_{1}, j_{2}, j_{3}, j_{4}$ są parami różne. Na mocy obserwacji z poprzedniego akapitu możemy bez ograniczenia ogólności rozumowania założyć, że $i_{k} \neq j_{k}$ dla $k=1,2,3$.

Mamy $q_{i_{1}} \equiv a q_{j_{1}}+b(\bmod p)$ i $q_{i_{2}} \equiv a q_{j_{2}}+b(\bmod p)$, skąd
$$
q_{i_{1}}-q_{i_{2}} \equiv a\left(q_{j_{1}}-q_{j_{2}}\right) \quad(\bmod p) .
$$
Analogicznie dowodzimy, że
$$
q_{i_{1}}-q_{i_{3}} \equiv a\left(q_{j_{1}}-q_{j_{3}}\right) \quad(\bmod p)
$$
Wobec tego
$\left(q_{i_{1}}-q_{i_{2}}\right)\left(q_{j_{1}}-q_{j_{3}}\right) \equiv a\left(q_{j_{1}}-q_{j_{2}}\right)\left(q_{j_{1}}-q_{j_{3}}\right) \equiv\left(q_{i_{1}}-q_{i_{3}}\right)\left(q_{j_{1}}-q_{j_{2}}\right)(\bmod p)$.

Mnożąc tę kongruencję przez $p_{i_{1}} p_{i_{2}} p_{i_{3}} p_{j_{1}} p_{j_{2}} p_{j_{3}}$ i wykorzystując to, że $p_{i} q_{i} \equiv 1(\bmod p)$ dla dowolnego $i$ otrzymujemy
$$
p_{i_{3}} p_{j_{2}}\left(p_{i_{2}}-p_{i_{1}}\right)\left(p_{j_{3}}-p_{j_{1}}\right) \equiv p_{i_{2}} p_{j_{3}}\left(p_{i_{3}}-p_{i_{1}}\right)\left(p_{j_{2}}-p_{j_{1}}\right) \quad(\bmod p)
$$
Wartości bezwzględne liczb stojących po obu stronach tej kongruencji są mniejsze od $\frac{1}{2} p$, gdyż z założeń zadania $p_{i}<\sqrt[4]{\frac{1}{2} p}$ dla każdego $i$. Te dwie liczby różnią się więc o nie więcej niż $p$ i dają taką samą resztę z dzielenia przez $p$, więc są równe. Zatem
$$
p_{i_{3}} p_{j_{2}}\left(p_{i_{2}}-p_{i_{1}}\right)\left(p_{j_{3}}-p_{j_{1}}\right)=p_{i_{2}} p_{j_{3}}\left(p_{i_{3}}-p_{i_{1}}\right)\left(p_{j_{2}}-p_{j_{1}}\right)
$$
Ponieważ liczba pierwsza $p_{i_{3}}$ nie jest dzielnikiem żadnej z liczb $p_{i_{2}}, p_{j_{3}}$, $p_{i_{3}}-p_{i_{1}}$, więc jest dzielnikiem liczby $p_{j_{2}}-p_{j_{1}}$. W szczególności
$$
p_{i_{3}} \leqslant\left|p_{j_{2}}-p_{j_{1}}\right|<\max \left\{p_{j_{1}}, p_{j_{2}}\right\} \leqslant \max \left\{p_{i_{1}}, p_{i_{2}}, p_{i_{3}}, p_{j_{1}}, p_{j_{2}}, p_{j_{3}}\right\}
$$
Analogicznie dowodzimy, że każda z liczb $p_{i_{1}}, p_{i_{2}}, p_{i_{3}}, p_{j_{1}}, p_{j_{2}}, p_{j_{3}}$ jest mniejsza od $\max \left\{p_{i_{1}}, p_{i_{2}}, p_{i_{3}}, p_{j_{1}}, p_{j_{2}}, p_{j_{3}}\right\}$. To daje sprzeczność, bo wśród dowolnych sześciu liczb istnieje największa.

statement: Let $n\ge4$ and suppose $p=n+1$ is prime. A set of $n$ cells of an $n\times n$ chessboard is called tactical if queens placed on these cells do not attack one another. Prove that $n-2$ tactical sets can cover every cell outside the board's two main diagonals.
solution:
Label rows and columns by $1,\ldots,p-1$. For each $a\in\{2,\ldots,p-2\}$, take
$$X_a=\{(i,j):j\equiv ai\pmod p,\ 1\le i,j\le p-1\}.$$
There is one cell in each column, and because $a$ is invertible modulo $p$, one in each row. If two cells shared a rising or falling diagonal, then $a(i-i')\equiv\pm(i-i')\pmod p$. Since $i\ne i'$, this would force $a\equiv\pm1$, excluded. Thus $X_a$ is tactical.

For a cell $(i,j)$ outside the main diagonals, the residue $a\equiv ji^{-1}\pmod p$ is neither $1$ nor $-1$, so the cell belongs to the corresponding $X_a$. These $p-3=n-2$ sets suffice.

statement:
For $n\ge2$ let $a_1,\ldots,a_n\in[0,1]$. Prove that there are $b_1,\ldots,b_n\in\{0,1\}$ such that every $1\le k\le\ell\le n$ satisfies
$$\left|\sum_{i=k}^{\ell}(a_i-b_i)\right|\le\frac n{n+1}.$$
solution:
Put $S_0=0$ and $S_j=a_1+\cdots+a_j$. On the unit circle, the at most $n+1$ fractional parts of $S_0,\ldots,S_n$ leave a gap of length at least $1/(n+1)$. Choose a rotation of the circle so that all these fractional parts lie in a closed interval of length at most $n/(n+1)$. Equivalently, there is a real number $c$ for which all remainders $\{S_j+c\}$ lie in such an interval.

Define $b_j=\lfloor S_j+c\rfloor-\lfloor S_{j-1}+c\rfloor$. Because $0\le S_j-S_{j-1}\le1$, each $b_j$ is 0 or 1. Finally
$$\sum_{j=k}^{\ell}(a_j-b_j)=\{S_\ell+c\}-\{S_{k-1}+c\},$$
and the right side has absolute value at most the length of the containing interval.

ratingReason: The main insight is to round every partial sum using a common offset chosen from the largest gap between fractional parts; this controls every interval simultaneously.

statement: In triangle $ABC$ with $AC<BC$, the incircle touches $AB$ and $AC$ at $D$ and $E$. The segment $CD$ meets the incircle again at $K$. Let $L$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $CD$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $DE$. If $H$ is the orthocentre of $KLM$, prove that $AH\perp HK$.
solution:
Because $AD=AE$, the line $AM$ is perpendicular to $DE$. Thus $A,L,D,M$ lie on the circle with diameter $AD$. The tangent-chord theorem gives, in directed angles,
$$\angle KLM=\angle DAM=90^\circ-\angle MDA=90^\circ-\angle EKD.$$
Hence $LM\perp EK$, so the altitude through $K$ of triangle $KLM$ is $KE$, and $H\in KE$. Since $MH\perp KL$, another angle comparison gives
$$\angle MHE=90^\circ-\angle EKD=90^\circ-\angle AEM=\angle MAE.$$
Therefore $A,H,E,M$ are concyclic. Since $AM\perp EM$, this circle has diameter $AE$, and $AH\perp HE=HK$.

ratingReason: The tangent-chord theorem first identifies one altitude of the auxiliary triangle; a second circle with a tangent segment as diameter gives the desired perpendicularity.

statement: Let $a_1,\ldots,a_k$ be distinct positive reals and set $S=\{\pm a_1,\ldots,\pm a_k\}$. For a positive integer $n$ and real $t$, let $N(t)$ count ordered $2n$-tuples from $S$ whose sum is $t$. Prove that $N(0)\ge N(t)$ for every real $t$.
solution:
Let $c(u)$ count ordered $n$-tuples from $S$ with sum $u$, setting it to zero for all other values. Only finitely many values are nonzero, and negating every entry gives $c(u)=c(-u)$. Splitting a tuple in half yields
$$N(0)=\sum_u c(u)^2,\qquad N(t)=\sum_u c(u)c(t-u).$$
The sums may be taken over the finite union of the supports involved. By Cauchy-Schwarz,
$$N(t)^2\le\left(\sum_u c(u)^2\right)\left(\sum_u c(t-u)^2\right)=N(0)^2.$$
Both counts are nonnegative, proving the claim.

ratingReason: Splitting a 2n-term sum into two halves converts the comparison into a correlation bound; the hidden Cauchy-Schwarz step needs a suitable counting function.

statement:
Distinct real numbers $a,b,c,d,e$ satisfy
$$ab+b=ac+a,\quad bc+c=bd+b,\quad cd+d=ce+c,\quad de+e=da+d.$$
Prove that $abcde=1$.
solution:
Rewrite the equations as $b(a+1)=a(c+1)$, $c(b+1)=b(d+1)$, $d(c+1)=c(e+1)$ and $e(d+1)=d(a+1)$. Distinctness implies $b,c,d\ne0$ and $a,c,d\ne-1$: a zero or a forbidden -1 would force two adjacent displayed variables equal. Multiplying and cancelling these nonzero factors yields the missing relation $e(b+1)=a(e+1)$.

The five equations now read
$$a(b-c)=a-b,\ b(c-d)=b-c,\ c(d-e)=c-d,\ d(e-a)=d-e,\ e(a-b)=e-a.$$
Multiply them and cancel the nonzero product $(a-b)(b-c)(c-d)(d-e)(e-a)$. The result is $abcde=1$.

ratingReason: Multiplying the four shifted-factor equations recovers a missing fifth relation; multiplying the resulting difference identities telescopes to the product.

statement: Let $I$ be the incentre of acute triangle $ABC$. A point $X$ lies on $BC$, on the same side of $AI$ as $B$, and $Y$ lies on the minor arc $AB$ of the circumcircle. Suppose $\angle AIX=\angle XYA=120^\circ$. Prove that $YI$ bisects $\angle XYA$.
solution:
Let $M$ be the midpoint of the minor arc $BC$. The arc-midpoint lemma gives $MB=MC=MI$. Construct equilateral triangle $IMZ$ on the side of $IM$ containing $X$. Then $I,X,Z$ are collinear. Put $T=XY\cap MZ$. Since $\angle XYA=120^\circ$ and the angle between $MA$ and $MZ$ is $60^\circ$, the cyclic angle criterion shows that $T$ lies on the circumcircle of $ABC$ (directed angles cover either intersection order).

The points $B,C,I,Z$ lie on the circle with centre $M$. Applying the power-of-a-point theorem at $X$ to this circle and to the circumcircle of $ABC$ gives
$$XI\cdot XZ=XB\cdot XC=XY\cdot XT.$$
Thus $XI/XY=XT/XZ$, and the corresponding included angles at $X$ agree. Triangles $IXY$ and $TXZ$ are similar, so $\angle XYI=\angle TZI=60^\circ$. Since $\angle XYA=120^\circ$, the claim follows.

statement: The prism $ABCA_1B_1C_1$ is right, and $ABC,A_1BC,AB_1C,ABC_1$ are acute triangles. Show that their four orthocentres and the centroid of $ABC$ lie on one sphere.
solution:
Let $H,M$ be the orthocentre and centroid of $ABC$, and put $T=M+\frac13\overrightarrow{AA_1}$. The point $T$ lies in each of the planes $A_1BC,AB_1C,ABC_1$: for example it divides $NA_1$ in ratio $1:2$, where $N$ is the midpoint of $BC$.

Let $H_1$ be the orthogonal projection of $H$ onto the plane $A_1BC$. Since $CH\perp AB$ and $CH$ lies in the base plane, $CH\perp BA_1$ also. Projection onto the plane preserves this perpendicularity to $BA_1$, so $CH_1\perp BA_1$. Similarly $BH_1\perp CA_1$. Thus $H_1$ is the orthocentre of $A_1BC$. In particular $HH_1\perp H_1T$, placing $H_1$ on the sphere with diameter $HT$. The same argument handles the other two lifted triangles. Finally $HM\perp MT$, so $M$ also lies on that sphere, as does $H$.

statement:
Call an integer-coefficient polynomial pair $(F,G)$ separating modulo 100 if
$$F(a,b)\equiv F(c,d),\quad G(a,b)\equiv G(c,d)\pmod {100}$$
implies $a\equiv c$ and $b\equiv d\pmod {100}$. Can both $(P,Q)$ and $(P-xy,Q+xy)$ be separating modulo 100?
solution:
No. A separating pair maps the $100^2$ residue pairs injectively, hence bijectively, to themselves. The parity of each polynomial value depends only on the input parity pair. Surjectivity therefore forces the four input parity pairs to map to all four output parity pairs exactly once.

For the two proposed pairs, the outputs modulo 2 coincide at $(0,0),(1,0),(0,1)$, while both coordinates change at $(1,1)$. If the first map permutes the four parity pairs, its three common outputs leave a unique fourth output; the changed fourth output cannot fill that same place. Thus the second map is not a permutation, a contradiction.

ratingReason: Injectivity modulo 100 must first be turned into a permutation of parity pairs; changing exactly one of four images then contradicts bijectivity.

statement: Write $1,2,\ldots,60$ in order. Two players alternately fill an unused gap with $+$, $-$ or $\times$; Igor moves first. Once all gaps are filled, evaluate the expression with usual precedence. Igor wins if it is divisible by 3. Which player can force a win?
solution:
Igor wins. First put a minus sign between 30 and 31. Pair each of the remaining 29 gaps in the first half with the corresponding gap in the second half. Reply in the paired gap, replacing $+$ by $-$, $-$ by $+$, and $\times$ by $\times$.

Modulo 3, corresponding entries in the two halves are equal. Multiplication blocks are consequently paired with equal residues, while their signs in the complete expression are opposite (including the first block, whose negative sign is the initial central move). The full expression is therefore 0 modulo 3.

statement: Twenty-five athletes compete in 25 events, each awarding exactly one gold medal. Each of 25 experts predicts a nonnegative integer medal count for every athlete, totalling 25. An expert succeeds if at least one predicted count is correct. What is the largest number of experts that can be guaranteed to succeed, whatever the actual results?
solution:
The answer is 24. Any single prediction can be defeated. If it predicts all ones, use outcome $(25,0,\ldots,0)$. Otherwise it has at least one zero; distribute all medals positively among exactly the athletes assigned zero. Every count then differs from its prediction. Thus guaranteeing all 25 is impossible.

For a construction, one expert predicts all ones. For each $i=1,\ldots,24$, another expert predicts one medal for athlete $i$, 24 for athlete 25, and zero for everyone else. Two of these latter experts cannot both fail: their two distinguished athletes would each need at least two medals, and the remaining 22 of the first 24 athletes would each need at least one, requiring at least 26 medals. If the all-ones expert fails, every actual count is either 0 or at least 2; there are at most 12 positive counts, hence at least 13 zeros. Every other expert predicts zero in 23 positions, so each then succeeds. In every case at most one expert fails.

statement: Players alternately write one capital English letter in an empty cell of a $100\times100$ board. Petr starts and wins if the completed board contains PETR in four consecutive cells, read left-to-right or top-to-bottom. Can Petr force a win?
solution:
No. His opponent always writes a letter outside PETR. When Petr writes P, try to occupy the cell immediately right; for E, the cell immediately left; for T, the cell immediately below; for R, the cell immediately above. If that cell is unavailable, fill any empty cell.

A horizontal PE can never be completed: after its first letter appears, the opponent occupies the position of the second, unless that position already contains an incompatible letter. The same reasoning forbids vertical TR. Every horizontal PETR contains horizontal PE, and every vertical PETR contains vertical TR, so Petr cannot win.

statement:
Determine all positive integers $n$ for which some positive even integer $a$ makes
$$\prod_{j=1}^n(a^j-1)$$
a perfect square.
solution:
The possible values are $n=1,2$: use $a=2$ and $a=8$, respectively.

For $n=3$, write the product as $(a-1)^3(a+1)(a^2+a+1)$. Since $a$ is even, $a+1$ is coprime to both other factors, so $a+1$ is a square. Modulo 3 this implies $a-1\not\equiv0$. Hence $\gcd(a-1,a^2+a+1)=\gcd(a-1,3)=1$, so $a^2+a+1$ must be a square. But it lies strictly between $a^2$ and $(a+1)^2$.

For $n\ge4$, choose $k\ge2$ with $2^k\le n<2^{k+1}$. Split the factor at index $2^k$ as
$$a^{2^k}-1=(a^{2^{k-1}}-1)(a^{2^{k-1}}+1).$$
Let $F=a^{2^{k-1}}+1$. It is coprime to the first factor because both are odd and differ by 2. For every other index $m\le n$, $2^k\nmid m$. The identity $\gcd(a^u-1,a^v-1)=a^{\gcd(u,v)}-1$ shows that any common divisor of $F$ and $a^m-1$ also divides $a^{2^{k-1}}-1$, so is 1. Thus $F$ is coprime to the remaining product and must itself be a square. But $a^{2^{k-1}}$ is already a positive square, and its successor is not. This contradiction finishes the proof.

ratingReason: The case n=3 needs coprime-factor reasoning; the general obstruction isolates a nonsquare factor at the highest power-of-two index.

statement: Arrange $1,2,\ldots,n$ in a row and record the gcd of each consecutive pair. What is the greatest possible number of distinct recorded values?
solution:
The answer is $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$. The gcd $d$ of two distinct entries cannot exceed $n/2$: the larger entry is at least $2d$.

For equality, partition the entries into chains $u,2u,4u,\ldots$ according to their odd part $u$, and concatenate these chains in any order. Every $d\le n/2$ is followed by $2d$ inside its chain, so the gcd $d$ occurs. For $n=1$ both the formula and the empty list give zero.

statement: Find the least integer $k$ such that every real polynomial $f$ of degree 100 admits a real polynomial $g$ of degree at most $k$ whose graph meets the graph of $f$ in exactly 100 points.
solution:
The answer is 98. Scale so that $f$ is monic, with coefficient $a$ at $x^{99}$. Choose 100 distinct real numbers $r_i$ with sum $-a$, and set $h(x)=\prod_i(x-r_i)$. The top two coefficients of $f,h$ coincide, so $g=f-h$ has degree at most 98; its intersections with $f$ are exactly the 100 chosen roots.

Degree at most 97 cannot always work. Take $f=x^{100}$. If $f-g$ had 100 distinct real roots $r_i$, Vieta would give $\sum r_i=\sum_{i<j}r_ir_j=0$. Thus $\sum r_i^2=(\sum r_i)^2-2\sum_{i<j}r_ir_j=0$, forcing all roots to be zero, a contradiction.

ratingReason: Matching the leading two coefficients constructs the upper bound; a sum-of-squares consequence of Vieta rules out one smaller degree.

statement: Place 100 distinct real numbers in $(0,1)$ around a circle. A move replaces the middle entry $b$ of three consecutive entries $a,b,c$ by $a-b+c$. What is the largest possible number of integer entries obtainable, with a suitable initial choice and finitely many moves?
solution:
The maximum is 50. A move swaps the two adjacent differences $a-b$ and $b-c$, leaving the other differences unchanged. Initially every adjacent difference is nonintegral, so this remains true. Two integer entries can therefore never be adjacent, giving the upper bound 50.

To attain it, choose distinct positive numbers $u_1,\ldots,u_{50}$ all close to $1/10$, with the adjacent sums $u_i+u_{i+1}$ distinct and close to $1/5$ (indices cyclic). For example choose $u_i=1/10+\varepsilon2^i$ with sufficiently small positive $\varepsilon$; distinct unordered pairs of powers of two have distinct sums. Alternate $u_i$ and $u_i+u_{i+1}$ around the circle. All 100 entries are distinct and in $(0,1)$. Replace each sum entry using its two neighbouring $u$'s. It becomes zero, and the 50 unaltered $u$ entries remain between the zeros.

statement: The diagonals of convex quadrilateral $ABCD$ meet at $E$. For the circles $(ABE)$ and $(CDE)$, their four points of contact with their two common external tangents lie on a circle $\omega$. Define $\gamma$ similarly from $(ADE)$ and $(BCE)$. Prove that $\omega$ and $\gamma$ have the same centre.
solution:
For any two circles with centres $U,V$, the four external-tangent contact points lie on a circle centred at the midpoint of $UV$: the two radii to a common tangent are parallel, and the midpoint of $UV$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining the two contact points; symmetry handles the other tangent.

Now denote the four circumcentres by $O_{AB},O_{BC},O_{CD},O_{DA}$. The line $O_{AB}O_{BC}$ is the perpendicular bisector of $BE$, and $O_{CD}O_{DA}$ is the perpendicular bisector of $DE$. Since $B,E,D$ are collinear, these two lines are parallel. The other pair of sides is similarly parallel, using $A,E,C$. Thus the four centres form a parallelogram. Its diagonals have the same midpoint, which by the first observation is the centre of both $\omega$ and $\gamma$.

statement: A king makes a closed tour of an $8\times8$ board, visiting each square exactly once before returning to the starting square on move $64$. A move is pleasant when the distance from the occupied square's centre to the board's centre decreases. What is the largest possible number of pleasant moves?
solution:
The maximum is $\boxed{44}$. Index squares by $(i,j)$ with $1\le i,j\le8$, and compare the squared-distance labels $D=(2i-9)^2+(2j-9)^2$. There are four squares of label $2$, eight of label $10$, thirty-two with label at least $50$, and twenty with label greater than $50$. All four moves leaving label $2$ are non-pleasant. At least four of the eight moves leaving label $10$ are non-pleasant, since only the four label-$2$ squares can be pleasant destinations. At least twelve moves entering the thirty-two squares of label at least $50$ are non-pleasant, since a pleasant such move must leave one of the twenty squares with larger label. These last moves do not leave labels $2$ or $10$: one king move from those squares has label at most $34$. Thus at least $4+4+12=20$ of the $64$ moves are non-pleasant.

For attainment, follow this explicit list of squares in order and return to its first entry: $(1,1); (1,2); (1,3); (1,4); (2,5); (1,5); (2,6); (1,7); (1,6); (2,7); (1,8); (2,8); (3,8); (4,8); (3,7); (4,7); (3,6); (4,6); (5,5); (6,5); (5,4); (6,3); (5,3); (6,2); (7,1); (7,2); (8,1); (8,2); (8,3); (8,4); (7,5); (6,4); (7,3); (7,4); (8,5); (7,6); (8,7); (8,6); (7,7); (8,8); (7,8); (6,8); (5,8); (6,7); (5,7); (6,6); (5,6); (4,5); (3,4); (2,3); (2,4); (3,5); (4,4); (4,3); (3,2); (2,1); (3,1); (4,1); (5,2); (6,1); (5,1); (4,2); (3,3); (2,2)$. Each square occurs once, successive squares (including last to first) are king-adjacent, and direct comparison of the labels gives $44$ decreases.

statement:
Find all positive integers $n$ for which positive integers $a,b$ satisfy both: no prime cube divides $a^2+b+3$, and
$$\frac{ab+3b+8}{a^2+b+3}=n.$$
solution:
Writing $D=a^2+b+3$, rearrangement gives
$$(a+3-n)D=(a+1)^3.$$
The factor $t=a+3-n$ is positive. For each prime $p$, the exponent of $p$ in $D$ is at most 2. If the exponent in $t$ were smaller than that in $a+1$, then the identity would force the exponent in $D$ to be at least 3, impossible. Hence $a+1\mid t=a+3-n$. Positivity gives $n\le2$. If $n=1$, it would say $a+1\mid a+2$, impossible for positive $a$. Thus $n=2$, realised by $a=b=2$, for which $D=9$.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of Auswahlwettbewerb zur Internationalen Mathematik-Olympiade 2022
ratingReason: Eliminating the denominator exposes a cube; the cube-free restriction converts that identity into a divisibility relation that sharply bounds n.
license: MathNet CC BY4.0; original contest rights retained where asserted

statement: Fix a positive integer $k$. Partition the $4k^2$ lattice points $(x,y)$ with $0\le x,y<2k$ into $k^2$ groups of four, each group forming a nondegenerate quadrilateral. What is the maximum sum of the quadrilateral areas?
solution:
Let $O=(k-\tfrac12,k-\tfrac12)$. For any quadrilateral with consecutive vertices $A_1,\ldots,A_4$, decomposition into triangles and $2uv\le u^2+v^2$ give
$$[A_1A_2A_3A_4]\le\frac12\sum_{i=1}^4 OA_i\,OA_{i+1}\le\frac12\sum_{i=1}^4 OA_i^2,$$
where indices are cyclic. Therefore the total is at most half the sum of $OA^2$ over all lattice points.

Rotation through $90^\circ$ about $O$ permutes the lattice set and has orbits of exactly four points. Each orbit forms a square centred at $O$, attaining equality in both estimates. Summing squared distances gives
$$\frac12\sum_{x,y=0}^{2k-1}\left[(x-k+\tfrac12)^2+(y-k+\tfrac12)^2\right]=\boxed{\frac{k^2(4k^2-1)}3}.$$
sourceName: MathNet transcription of Auswahlwettbewerb zur Internationalen Mathematik-Olympiade 2022
ratingReason: The main insight bounds every quadrilateral by half the sum of squared distances to a common centre; rotation orbits attain the bound simultaneously.
license: MathNet CC BY4.0; original contest rights retained where asserted

statement:
Let $S$ be an infinite set of positive integers. Suppose four distinct elements $v,w,x,y$ satisfy $\gcd(v,w)\ne\gcd(x,y)$. Prove that some distinct $a,b,c\in S$ satisfy
$$\gcd(a,b)=\gcd(a,c)\ne\gcd(b,c).$$
solution:
Colour each edge between two members of $S$ by their gcd. Every vertex sees finitely many colours, since its gcds divide that vertex. Some vertex $a$ sees two colours: otherwise all edges incident to each vertex would have one colour, forcing every edge in the complete graph to share a colour.

Choose an infinite set $T$ with all edges from $a$ coloured $g$, and a vertex $d$ with edge $ad$ coloured $h\ne g$. There are distinct $b,c\in T$ such that $bd,cd$ have the same colour $q$. If $q=g$, triangle $abd$ has exactly two colours. If $q\ne g$, consider the colour of $bc$: unless it is $g$, triangle $abc$ has exactly two colours; if it is $g$, triangle $bcd$ has exactly two colours. In every case, relabel the vertices of the resulting triangle to obtain the required equality and inequality.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of Auswahlwettbewerb zur Internationalen Mathematik-Olympiade 2022
ratingReason: Two applications of the infinite pigeonhole principle create a four-vertex pattern; one then has to prove that this pattern forces exactly two gcd values on a triangle.

statement:
Real numbers $a_1,\ldots,a_{2022}\ge1$ satisfy $|a_i-a_j|\ge1$ whenever $i\ne j$. Find the smallest possible value of
$$\sum_{i=1}^{2022}\left\lfloor\frac{a_i}{i}\right\rfloor.$$
solution:
The answer is 11. Replacing the smallest entry by 1, the next by 2, and so on cannot increase the sum, so it suffices to bound sums for distinct positive integers.

We prove that for $2^t$ distinct positive integers the first $2^t$ terms have sum at least $t+1$. The base $t=0$ is clear. Let $h=2^{t-1}$ and choose an entry at least $2h$. If its index exceeds $h$, it contributes at least 1 beyond the first half, which contributes at least $t$ by induction. If its index $i$ is at most $h$, choose an integer $b\in\{1,\ldots,h\}$ absent from that half. Replacing the large entry by $b$ decreases its floor by at least 1, because the original entry is at least $b+i$. The modified half still has distinct positive entries, so its sum is at least $t$, giving at least $t+1$ before replacement.

The first 1024 terms therefore contribute at least 11. For equality, set $a_i=i-1$ when $i$ is not a power of two, and $a_{2^s}=2^{s+1}-1$. All entries are distinct. Only the eleven power-of-two positions contribute, each contributing 1.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of Auswahlwettbewerb zur Internationalen Mathematik-Olympiade 2022
ratingReason: Ordering reduces to distinct integers; a dyadic induction with replacement of a large entry proves the lower bound, and an unusual permutation-like construction achieves it.

statement: In parallelogram $ABCD$, suppose $AC=BC$. Take $P$ on ray $AB$ beyond $B$. The circle $(ACD)$ meets $PD$ again at $Q$, and the circle $(APQ)$ meets $PC$ again at $R$. Prove that $CD,AQ,BR$ are concurrent.
solution:
Use directed angles modulo $180^\circ$. The length condition and parallel sides give
$$\angle BAC=\angle CBA=\angle DCA=\angle ADC.$$
Let $S=AQ\cap CD$. Since $CD\parallel AP$ and $A,P,Q,R$ are cyclic, $\angle CSQ=\angle PAQ=\angle CRQ$, so $C,S,R,Q$ are cyclic. Also
$$\angle CRA=-\angle ARP=\angle DQA=\angle DCA=\angle CBA,$$
so $A,B,R,C$ are cyclic. It follows that
$$\angle SRC=\angle SQC=\angle ADC=\angle BAC=\angle BRP.$$
As $P,R,C$ are collinear, this says $S,R,B$ are collinear, proving concurrence.

statement: Find all positive integer quadruples $(a,b,c,d)$ such that $a^2+b^2=c^2+d^2$ and $ac+bd$ divides $a^2+b^2$.
solution:
Set $a^2+b^2=k(ac+bd)$ for a positive integer $k$. The identity
$$(ac+bd)^2+(ad-bc)^2=(a^2+b^2)(c^2+d^2)$$
gives $((ad-bc)/(ac+bd))^2=k^2-1$. A rational number whose square is an integer must itself be an integer, so $k^2-1$ is a square. This forces $k=1$, since for $k\ge2$ it lies strictly between $(k-1)^2$ and $k^2$. Thus $ad=bc$, and equality of the two sums of squares forces $(a,b)=(c,d)$. All quadruples $(a,b,a,b)$ work.

ratingReason: A two-square identity converts the integer quotient into a rational square root between successive squares, forcing equality.

statement: A $3\times3\times3$ cube consists of 27 unit cubes, each containing an initially unlit bulb. Pressing any unit cube except the central one toggles its bulb and the bulbs in all face-adjacent cubes. Decide whether one can obtain (a) all bulbs lit; (b) all except the central bulb lit; (c) only the central bulb lit.
solution:
Consider the seven bulbs consisting of the cube's centre and the six face-centre cubes. Every permitted press toggles either zero or two of these seven: a face-centre press toggles itself and the centre; an edge-centre press toggles two face centres; a corner press toggles none. Their lit-count parity stays even. Targets (a) and (c) have an odd count, so are impossible.

For (b), press all twelve edge-centre cubes, then all six face-centre cubes. Each corner is toggled three times; each edge centre once plus twice; each face centre four times plus once; and the centre six times. Thus precisely the central bulb remains off.

ratingReason: The invariant is the parity of the seven central lights; the possible target also needs an explicit sequence of presses.

statement: In an acute scalene triangle $ABC$, let $I,H$ be the incentre and orthocentre, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$. Choose $D,E$ on the line $AH$ so that $MD\parallel CI$ and $ME\perp CI$. Prove $AE=DH$.
solution: Let $N$ be the midpoint of $DE$. Since $MD\perp ME$, $N$ is the circumcentre of the right triangle $DME$. The angle between $DE$ and $EM$ equals the angle between their perpendiculars $BC$ and $CI$, namely half of $\angle BCA$. The corresponding central angle between $ND$ and $NM$ therefore equals $\angle BCA$. The angle between $AH$ and $BH$ also equals $\angle BCA$, so $MN\parallel BH$ (interpreting angles as directed angles if an intersection is on an extension). In triangle $ABH$, the line through midpoint $M$ parallel to $BH$ meets $AH$ at its midpoint. Hence $N$ is the midpoint of both $AH$ and $DE$. Reflection in $N$ exchanges $A,H$ and $D,E$, giving $AE=HD$.

statement: Sean $x_1 \le x_2 \le x_3 \le x_4$ cuatro números reales. Demuestra que existen $P(x)$ y $Q(x)$ polinomios de grado dos con coeficientes reales tales que $x_1, x_2, x_3$ y $x_4$ son las raíces de $P(Q(x))$ si y solamente si $x_1 + x_4 = x_2 + x_3$.
solution:
Supongamos que las raíces de $P(x)$ son $r$ y $s$. Entonces las raíces de $P(Q(x))$ son las raíces de $Q(x) - r$ y de $Q(x) - s$. Por las relaciones de Cardano, la suma de las raíces de $Q(x) - r$ es la misma que la de $Q(x) - s$, con lo que las raíces de $P(Q(x))$ necesariamente satisfacen que la suma de dos de ellas coincide con la suma de las otras dos.

Vamos a demostrar ahora el recíproco. Consideremos una cuaterna $(x_1, x_2, x_3, x_4)$ con $x_1 + x_4 = x_2 + x_3$. Por tanto, queremos elegir $(Q(x), r, s)$ de manera que
$$
Q(x) - r = (x - x_1)(x - x_4), \quad Q(x) - s = (x - x_2)(x - x_3).
$$
Para ello, pongamos $Q(x) = x^2 - (x_1 + x_4)x$. La condición se reescribe por tanto como
$$
r = -x_1x_4, \quad s = -x_2x_3,
$$
y hemos acabado.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of LIX Olimpiada Matemática Española
ratingReason: The axis of symmetry of the inner quadratic pairs the four real roots; constructing two quadratics from the paired roots is then immediate.

statement: A row has 203 cells. Initially all 203 tokens occupy the leftmost cell. One move transfers either one token or exactly twenty tokens from one cell to an adjacent cell. After 2023 moves every cell contains one token. Prove that some token moved left at least nine times.
solution:
For the boundary with exactly $n$ cells to its right, the net number of tokens crossing rightward is $n$. Write $n=20q+r$, $0\le r<20$. If the net numbers of twenty-token and single-token crossings are $u,v$, then $20u+v=n$, and the number of moves is at least $|u|+|v|$. Its minimum is
$$q+\min(r,21-r).$$
Summing for $n=1,\ldots,202$ gives 2023: over $n=0,\ldots,199$ the total is $20(0+\cdots+9)+10\cdot109=1990$, and the last three values contribute $10+11+12=33$. Thus every boundary attains its minimum.

In particular the boundary with eleven cells to its right is crossed in exactly ten moves: once by twenty tokens rightwards and nine times by individual tokens leftwards. Consider those twenty tokens just after their shared rightward move. They all occupy the eleventh cell counted from the right. Since their final cells are distinct, one finishes at least as far left as the twentieth cell counted from the right. That token must subsequently make at least nine leftward steps, as required.

ratingReason: Summing sharp crossing-cost bounds forces equality at every boundary; a second pigeonhole argument then tracks one token far enough backwards.

statement: In scalene triangle $ABC$, the angle bisector $AI$ meets the circumcircle again at $D$, where $I$ is the incentre. Reflect $I$ in $D$ to obtain $J$. Let $E,F$ lie on line $BC$ with $IE,JF\perp AI$. Let $G,H$ be the perpendicular feet of $I,J$ on $AE,AF$, respectively. Prove $BG=CH$.
solution:
The arc-midpoint lemma gives $DB=DC=DI=DJ$, and identifies $J$ as the $A$-excentre. Thus the circle $BICJ$ has diameter $IJ$, with tangents $IE,JF$. Taking powers of $E$ and $F$, and using the right triangles $AIE,AJF$, gives
$$EB\cdot EC=EI^2=EA\cdot EG,\qquad FB\cdot FC=FJ^2=FA\cdot FH.$$
Consequently $G,H$ lie on the circumcircle of $ABC$.

Put $K=AI\cap BC$. The internal and external angle-bisector theorems in triangle $ABK$ give $IA/IK=JA/JK$. Similarity of $KIE$ and $KJF$ then gives $IA/JA=IE/JF$. The right triangles $AIE$ and $AJF$ are therefore similar, with their altitude feet $G,H$ corresponding. Hence $AG/AE=AH/AF$, so $GH\parallel EF\parallel BC$. The cyclic quadrilateral $BCHG$ is an isosceles trapezium, yielding $BG=CH$.

ratingReason: Recognising the reflected incentre as the excentre permits two power-of-a-point calculations; a separate bisector-ratio similarity supplies the final parallelism.

statement: Find all monic polynomials $P$ for which $P(x+1)$ divides $P(x)^2-1$.
solution:
The solutions are $P=1$ and $P(x)=x-c$, with $c$ any constant in the coefficient field. Both satisfy the condition.

For a nonconstant monic polynomial, choose a complex root $c$ with least real part, and list all roots with multiplicities as $c,r_2,\ldots,r_n$. Divisibility gives $P(c-1)=\pm1$. But $\Re(c-1-r_i)\le-1$, hence $|c-1-r_i|\ge1$; the product of these moduli is 1, so equality holds for every $i$. Equality forces $r_i=c$. Thus $P=(x-c)^n$. Now $P(x)^2-1=(x-c)^{2n}-1$ has a simple root at $x=c-1$, whereas $P(x+1)$ has multiplicity $n$ there. Therefore $n=1$.

statement: Дат је троугао $ABC$. Тачке $D$ и $E$ на правој $AB$ су такве да је $AD = AC$ и $BE = BC$, уз распоред $D-A-B-E$. Описане кружнице троуглова $DBC$ и $EAC$ секу се у тачки $X \neq C$, а описане кружнице троуглова $DEC$ и $ABC$ секу се у тачки $Y \neq C$. Ако важи $DY + EY = 2XY$, одредити $\angle ACB$.
solution:
Нека је $I_{c}$ центар приписаног круга $\triangle ABC$ наспрам темена $C$. Тада је $AI_{c}$ симетрала угла $CAD$, одакле је $\triangle I_{c}AD \cong \triangle I_{c}AC$. Следи да је $\angle I_{c}DB = \angle I_{c}DA = \angle I_{c}CA = \angle I_{c}CB$, па $I_{c}$ лежи на кругу $BCD$. Слично, $I_{c}$ лежи на кругу $ACE$, што значи да је $X \equiv I_{c}$. Такође, како је $XD = XC$ и аналогно $XE = XC$, тачка $X$ је центар круга $CDEY$.

Даље, $\angle DYA = \angle CYA - \angle CYD = \angle CBA - \angle CED = \angle CED = \angle CXA = \angle DXA$ и слично $\angle EYB = \angle EXB$. Зато посматрајмо тачку $X'$ симетричну тачки $X$ у односу на $AB$. Због $\angle DX'A = \angle DYA$ ова тачка лежи на кругу $ADY$, а аналогно и на кругу $BEY$.

Ако је $\angle C < 60^{\circ}$, онда је $\angle AX'B = \angle AXB = 90^{\circ} - \frac{1}{2} \angle C > \angle C = \angle AYB$, па тачка $X'$ лежи унутар $\triangle ABY$, а самим тим и унутар $\triangle DEY$. Следи да је $DY + EY > DX' + EX' = DX + EX = 2XY$. Слично, ако је $\angle C > 60^{\circ}$, тачка $Y$ лежи унутар $\triangle DEX$, те је тада $DY + EY < 2XY$. Према томе, ако је $DY + EY = 2XY$, мора бити $\angle C = 60^{\circ}$, а тада је $X' \equiv Y$ па заиста важи једнакост.


Друго решење. Углове троугла $ABC$ означавамо уобичајено са $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$. Као у првом решењу, тачке $C, D, E, Y$ леже на кругу са центром $X$. Такође, због $\angle CYD = \angle CED = \frac{\beta}{2}$, права $DY$ садржи средиште $N$ лука $AC$ круга $ABC$.

Означимо $\angle YDE = x$ и $\angle YED = y$. Услов $DY + EY = 2XY$ даје $\sin x + \sin y = \sin x + \sin \left(90^{\circ} - \frac{\gamma}{2} - x\right) = 1$.

$$
\left(1 - \sin \frac{\gamma}{2}\right) \sin x + \cos \frac{\gamma}{2} \cos x = 1
$$

С друге стране, синусна теорема у $\triangle ADN$ даје $2 \sin x \sin \frac{\alpha + \gamma}{2} = \cos \left(\frac{\alpha - \gamma}{2} - x\right)$, одакле следи $\operatorname{tg} x = \frac{\cos \frac{\alpha - \gamma}{2}}{2 \sin \frac{\alpha + \gamma}{2} - \sin \frac{\alpha - \gamma}{2}}$. Одавде налазимо
$$
\sin x = \frac{\cos \frac{\alpha - \gamma}{2}}{\sqrt{3 - 2 \cos \gamma + 4 \sin \frac{\gamma}{2} \cos \varphi}}, \quad \cos x = \frac{2 \sin \frac{\alpha + \gamma}{2} - \sin \frac{\alpha - \gamma}{2}}{\sqrt{3 - 2 \cos \gamma + 4 \sin \frac{\gamma}{2} \cos \varphi}}
$$
где је $\varphi = \alpha + \frac{\gamma}{2} - 90^{\circ} = \frac{\alpha - \beta}{2}$. Заменом у једначину (*) добијамо
$$
2 \cos \frac{3\gamma - 180^{\circ}}{4} \cos \frac{\varphi}{2} = \sqrt{3 - 2 \cos \gamma + 4 \sin \frac{\gamma}{2} \cos \varphi}
$$
што се након квадрирања своди на
$$
\cos \varphi = \frac{2 - 2 \cos \gamma - \sin \frac{3\gamma}{2}}{1 - 4 \sin \frac{\gamma}{2} + \sin \frac{3\gamma}{2}} = \frac{-3t + 4t^{2} + 4t^{3}}{1 - t - 4t^{3}}, \quad \text{где је} \quad t = \sin \frac{\gamma}{2}
$$
Ако је $\gamma \neq 60^{\circ}$, скраћивање $2t - 1 \neq 0$ даје $\cos \varphi = -\frac{2t^{2} + 3t}{2t^{2} + t + 1} < 0$, што је немогуће. Према томе, мора бити $\gamma = 60^{\circ}$.

statement:
For a positive integer $n$, let $v_2(n)$ be the exponent of 2 in its prime factorisation. Suppose $f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ satisfies $f(x)\le3x$ and
$$v_2(f(x)+f(y))=v_2(x+y)$$
for all positive integers $x,y$. Prove that every positive multiple of 3 is attained by $f$ exactly once.
solution:
Taking $x=y$ gives $v_2(f(x))=v_2(x)$. Also, if $x\not\equiv y\pmod{2^k}$, choose positive $z\equiv-x\pmod{2^k}$. Then $f(x)+f(z)$ is divisible by $2^k$, whereas $f(y)+f(z)$ is not. Hence $f(x)\not\equiv f(y)\pmod{2^k}$. In particular $f$ is injective.

First let $a$ be odd, and choose $k$ with $2^{k-1}<3a<2^k$. The odd inputs below $2^k$ have all distinct odd output residues modulo $2^k$, so some odd $x<2^k$ has $f(x)\equiv3a\pmod{2^k}$. If $f(x)\ne3a$, then $f(x)>2^k$. The valuation condition gives
$$f(x)+f(2^k-x)\equiv2^k\pmod{2^{k+1}},$$
so this positive sum is at least $3\cdot2^k$. The upper bounds make it at most $3\cdot2^k$, forcing equality and $f(x)=3x$. Thus $3x\equiv3a\pmod{2^k}$, and $x=a$, contradicting $f(x)\ne3a$. Therefore $f(x)=3a$.

For general $a=2^tu$ with $u$ odd, apply this argument to $g(x)=f(2^tx)/2^t$, which is integer-valued and satisfies the same two conditions. This proves existence, while the previously established injectivity proves uniqueness.

statement:
Дат је природан број $k$. Посматрајмо следећу игру на бесконачној једнодимензионалној табли. На почетку игре, на поља постављамо укупно $n$ жетона, при чему може бити више жетона на истом пољу. Након тога, у сваком потезу извршавамо једну од следећих операција:
$(1^{\circ})$ бирамо два суседна поља која су оба непразна и са једног од њих преносимо све жетоне на друго;
$(2^{\circ})$ бирамо поље са бар два жетона и са њега премештамо по један жетон $k$ поља улево и $k$ поља удесно.

a. Ако је $n \leqslant k+1$, доказати да ће се извршити само коначно много потеза.

б. За које вредности $k$ се може одабрати $n$ и поставити $n$ жетона тако да буде могућ бесконачан низ потеза?
solution:
(a) Потезе врсте $(1^{\circ})$ зваћемо скупљањем, а потезе врсте $(2^{\circ})$ сејањем. Поља нумеришемо редом бројевима $\ldots, -1, 0, 1, 2, \ldots$. Поља се могу поделити на $k$ класа по модулу $k$, тако да при сејању жетони не мењају своју класу.

Претпоставимо прво да у једној од класа нема ниједног жетона. Поља ове класе деле таблу на блокове дужине $k-1$, које опет нумеришемо целим бројевима. Како приликом скупљања ниједан жетон не излази из свог блока, унутар сваког блока може се извршити само коначно много узастопних скупљања. С друге стране, при сваком сејању се из неког блока $i$ пребацује по један жетон у блокове $i-1$ и $i+1$. Овако се задатак своди на следећи.

Лема. Нека се у сваком кораку бира $i$ и из блока $i$ премешта по један жетон у блокове $i-1$ и $i+1$. Тада се игра завршава у коначно много корака.

Доказ. Кад год нека два суседна блока $x$ и $x+1$ по први пут размене жетон, доделимо овом жетону број $x$. Приликом сваке следеће размене између ових двају блокова можемо сматрати да се размењује тај исти жетон. Овако сваки жетон само циркулише између два суседна блока. Следи да ће највише $n$ парова блокова икада разменити жетоне. Међутим, ако неки блок сеје жетоне бесконачно много пута, онда то мора да важи и за суседне блокове (иначе би се у њима гомилало бесконачно много жетона), а индукцијом и за све блокове, што је немогуће.

Остаје случај када се ниједна класа поља никад не испразни. Тада се увек у једној класи налазе два жетона, а у осталима по један. Сејања и скупљања се врше из класе са два жетона. Нека се у неком тренутку сеје са поља $p$ у $i$-тој класи (на коме су два жетона) на поља $p-k$ и $p+k$. Следи скупљање, и то без смањења општости удесно ка ($i+1$)-тој класи - са поља $p \pm k$ на поље $p \pm k+1$. Затим се из овог поља сеје на поља $p+1$ и $p \pm 2k+1$. Следи скупљање из ($i+1$)-те класе, али не у $i$-ту, јер је у њој једини жетон остао на пољу $p \mp k$. Дакле, сада се скупља у $(i+2)$-ту класу. Закључујемо да се наизменично сеје и скупља, при чему се класа из које се сеје и скупља циклично помера за један удесно. Може се сматрати без умањења општости да је жетон који се скупља увек исти - назовимо га црним. Црни жетон периодично учествује у сејању из сваке класе, дакле са свим осталим жетонима.

При сваком сејању црни жетон баца други жетон $k$ поља на једну страну, а себе $k$ поља на другу. Тако се у сваком циклусу од $k$ сејања позиција најлевљег жетона помера бар $k$ поља улево, а најдешњег бар $k$ поља удесно, те се опсег игре увећава за бар $2k$. Међутим, у току једног циклуса црни жетон не може прећи пут дужи од $k(k+1)$, па након $\frac{k+1}{2}$ циклуса он више не може стићи од најлевљег до најдешњег, што је коначна контрадикција.


(б) За свако $k$ даћемо пример периодичне (и самим тим бесконачне) игре. Посматрајмо $5k$ узастопних поља означених редом бројевима $1,2, \ldots, 5k$, свако са по једним жетоном. Делимо их на групе од по $k$ поља:
$$
1,1, \cdots, 1,1 \quad 1,1, \cdots, 1,1 \quad 1,1, \cdots, 1,1 \quad 1,1, \cdots, 1,1 \quad 1,1, \cdots, 1,1
$$
Почињемо скупљањем жетона са поља $1, \ldots, k$ на поље $k+1$. Затим, за $i=1,2, \ldots, k$, са поља $k+i$ једном сејемо, а преостале жетоне с тог поља скупљамо на поље $k+i+1$ (осим за $i=k$). Након $i$-тог циклуса стање је овакво:
$$
\underbrace{1,1, \ldots, 1}_i, 0,0, \ldots, 0 \quad \underbrace{0,0, \ldots, 0}_i, k+1-i, 1,1, \ldots, 1 \quad \underbrace{2,2, \ldots, 2}_i, 1,1, \ldots, 1 \quad 1,1, \cdots, 1,1 \quad 1,1, \cdots, 1,1
$$
Када аналогне потезе одиграмо и здесна, добићемо стање
$$
1,1, \cdots, 1,1 \quad 0,0, \cdots, 0,0 \quad 3,3, \cdots, 3,3 \quad 0,0, \cdots, 0,0 \quad 1,1, \cdots, 1,1
$$
Најзад, ако сада посејемо по једном са сваког од поља $2k+1, \ldots, 3k$, добијамо конфигурацију идентичну полазној.

statement: An acute triangle $ABC$ has circumcircle $\omega$. A circle centred at $A$ meets the minor arcs $AB$ and $AC$ at $D,E$, respectively. Suppose $K=BE\cap CD$ also lies on the circle centred at $A$. Prove $AK\perp BC$.
solution:
Use directed angles. Since $D,E,K$ lie on a circle centred at $A$,
$$\angle DAK=2\angle DEK.$$
Because $E,K,B$ are collinear and $A,B,D,E$ are cyclic, $\angle DEK=\angle DEB=\angle DAB$. Thus $AB$ bisects the angle between $AD$ and $AK$. As $AD=AK$, this bisector is perpendicular to $DK=DC$. Similarly $AC\perp EK=EB$. Therefore $K$ is the orthocentre of triangle $ABC$, and its third altitude is $AK\perp BC$.

ratingReason: A central-angle relation reveals that AB bisects the angle between two equal radii; this identifies two altitudes and hence the orthocentre.
notes: The source transcription mislabels a central angle; the corrected argument is written explicitly.

statement:
(A) Prove that for all real numbers $\kappa, \lambda, \mu$ holds the following inequality:
$$ (\kappa + \lambda + \mu)^2 \ge 3(\kappa\lambda + \lambda\mu + \mu\kappa). $$
When is equality valid?

(B) Let $x, y, z$ be positive real numbers and let $\alpha, \beta$ be real numbers such that
$$
\alpha(x + y + z) = \beta(xy + yz + zx) = xyz.
$$
Prove that $\alpha \ge 3\beta^2$. When is equality valid?
solution:
(A) It is enough to prove
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \kappa^2 + \lambda^2 + \mu^2 + 2\kappa\lambda + 2\lambda\mu + 2\mu\kappa \ge 3\kappa\lambda + 3\lambda\mu + 3\mu\kappa \\
\Leftrightarrow & \kappa^2 + \lambda^2 + \mu^2 - \kappa\lambda - \lambda\mu - \mu\kappa \ge 0 \\
\Leftrightarrow & (\kappa - \lambda)^2 + (\lambda - \mu)^2 + (\mu - \kappa)^2 \ge 0,
\end{aligned}
$$
which is valid for all real numbers $\kappa, \lambda, \mu$.
Equality holds if and only if $\kappa = \lambda = \mu$.

(B) From the given relation we get:
$$
\frac{1}{\alpha} = \frac{1}{xy} + \frac{1}{yz} + \frac{1}{zx} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{1}{\beta} = \frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{z}.
$$
Thus we have $\alpha, \beta > 0$ and from question (A) by putting $\kappa = \frac{1}{x}, \lambda = \frac{1}{y}, \mu = \frac{1}{z}$, we get
$$
\frac{1}{\beta^2} = \left(\frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{z}\right)^2 \ge 3 \left(\frac{1}{xy} + \frac{1}{yz} + \frac{1}{zx}\right) \Rightarrow \alpha \ge 3\beta^2.
$$
Equality holds if and only if $x = y = z$.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of HELLENIC MATHEMATICAL COMPETITIONS
ratingReason: Part A is the standard three-variable sum of squares, and the suggested reciprocal substitution proves part B directly.

statement: In a convex pentagon $ABCDE$, $\angle ABC=\angle AED=90^\circ$. The midpoint of $CD$ is the circumcenter of $ABE$. If $O$ is the circumcenter of $ACD$ and $N$ is the midpoint of $BE$, prove that $A,O,N$ are collinear.
solution: Take $A$ as the vector origin, with lower-case letters denoting position vectors. Put $U=c\cdot c$, $V=d\cdot d$ and $t=c\cdot d$. The circumcenter condition gives $b\cdot b=(c+d)\cdot b$, while the right angle at $B$ gives $b\cdot b=c\cdot b$. Hence $d\cdot b=0$. Since $b\ne0$, these conditions identify the projection $$b=c-\frac tVd.$$ Similarly $$e=d-\frac tUc.$$ Thus, writing $\Delta=UV-t^2>0$, $$n\cdot c=\frac{\Delta}{2V},\qquad n\cdot d=\frac{\Delta}{2U}.$$ On the other hand, $o\cdot c=U/2$ and $o\cdot d=V/2$. Since $c,d$ are independent, these dot products imply $$n=\frac{\Delta}{UV}o.$$ Therefore $A,N,O$ are collinear.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of HELLENIC MATHEMATICAL COMPETITIONS
ratingReason: The shared circumcenter and two right angles give orthogonal projection formulas for B and E; comparing their midpoint dot products with those of the second circumcenter proves collinearity.
notes: Independent vector proof resolves the previously missing solution; source is the Hellenic Mathematical Society 2023–24 booklet, Selection Examination, Seniors problem 2.
license: Original contest rights retained; concise paraphrase and original exposition.

statement: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC < BC$ and circumcircle $\Gamma_1$ of center $O$. We consider the circle $\Gamma_2$ with center $D$ lying on the circle $\Gamma_1$, and tangent to the line $BC$ at the point $E$ and tangent to the extension of the side $AB$ at point $F$. The circles $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2$ intersect at the points $K$ and $G$ (the point $K$ lies in the interior of the triangle $BFE$). If the line $KG$ intersects the lines $FE$ and $CD$ at the points $M$ and $N$, respectively, prove that the quadrilateral $BCNM$ is cyclic.
solution:
Let $r$ be the radius of $\Gamma_2$. The right angles at $E,F$ show that $B,E,D,F$ are cyclic; call this circle $\Gamma_3$. The radical axes of $(\Gamma_2,\Gamma_3)$ and $(\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2)$ are $EF$ and $KG$, meeting at $M$. Thus $M$ is on the third radical axis $BD$.

Use directed lengths on the relevant lines. Equality of the powers of $M$ with respect to $\Gamma_2$ and $\Gamma_3$ gives $MD^2-r^2=MD\cdot MB$, and hence $DM\cdot DB=r^2$. Similarly, equality of the powers of $N$ with respect to $\Gamma_2$ and $\Gamma_1$ gives $ND^2-r^2=ND\cdot NC$, hence $DN\cdot DC=r^2$. Therefore $DB\cdot DM=DC\cdot DN$, which by the converse of the secant-power theorem proves that $B,C,N,M$ are cyclic.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of HELLENIC MATHEMATICAL COMPETITIONS
ratingReason: The three-circle radical centre identifies M on BD; equal inversion products then give the requested cyclic quadrilateral.

statement:
Prove that there is an infinite number of triads of positive integers $(x, y, z)$ such that
$$
x^2 + y^2 + z^2 + xy + yz + zx = 6xyz.
$$
solution:
Treat the equation as a quadratic in $z$:
$$z^2-(6xy-x-y)z+(x^2+y^2+xy)=0.$$
Its other root is $z'=6xy-x-y-z$, an integer, and $zz'=x^2+y^2+xy$. Starting from $(1,1,1)$, root replacement gives $(3,1,1)$ and then $(13,3,1)$.

Now suppose $x>y>z>0$ is a solution. Replace its smallest coordinate $z$ by $z'$. Then
$$z'-x=\frac{x(x-z)+y^2+xy}{z}>0.$$
Thus $(z',x,y)$ is a positive integer solution with a strictly larger maximum. Repeating produces infinitely many distinct solutions.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of HELLENIC MATHEMATICAL COMPETITIONS
ratingReason: Viewing the equation as a quadratic allows a root replacement; the construction must prove the new coordinate strictly exceeds the previous maximum.
notes: The exposition corrects an extra squared factor in the transcribed quadratic rearrangement.

statement:
(i) If $x$, $y$ are positive real numbers, prove that:
$$
\frac{4}{x+y} \le \frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y}.
$$

(ii) If $\alpha$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, $\delta$ are positive real numbers, prove that
$$
\frac{2}{(\alpha + \beta)(\gamma + \delta) + (\beta + \gamma)(\alpha + \delta)} \le \frac{1}{(\alpha + \gamma)(\beta + \delta) + 4\alpha\gamma} + \frac{1}{(\alpha + \gamma)(\beta + \delta) + 4\beta\delta}.
$$
Determine when equality holds.
solution:
(i) Since $x$, $y$ are positive real numbers, we have:
$$
\frac{4}{x+y} \le \frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y} \Leftrightarrow \frac{4}{x+y} \le \frac{x+y}{xy} \Leftrightarrow (x+y)^2 \ge 4xy \Leftrightarrow (x-y)^2 \ge 0.
$$

(ii)
Let
$$
x = (\alpha + \gamma)(\beta + \delta) + 4\alpha\gamma, \quad y = (\alpha + \gamma)(\beta + \delta) + 4\beta\delta,
$$
and thus:
$$
\begin{aligned}
x + y &= 2(\alpha + \gamma)(\beta + \delta) + 4(\alpha\gamma + \beta\delta) \\
(\alpha + \beta)(\gamma + \delta) + (\beta + \gamma)(\alpha + \delta) &= \alpha\gamma + \alpha\delta + \beta\gamma + \beta\delta + \alpha\beta + \beta\delta + \alpha\gamma + \gamma\delta \\
&= (\alpha\beta + \alpha\delta + \beta\gamma + \gamma\delta) + 2(\alpha\gamma + \beta\delta) \\
&= (\alpha + \gamma)(\beta + \delta) + 2(\alpha\gamma + \beta\delta) = \frac{x+y}{2}
\end{aligned}
$$
Therefore the inequality becomes
$$
\frac{4}{x+y} \le \frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y},
$$
which is valid because of (i).

The equality holds if and only if $x = y \Leftrightarrow x - y = 0 \Leftrightarrow \alpha\gamma = \beta\delta$.

ratingReason: The denominators sum to twice the left denominator, so the second part is exactly the two-variable inequality supplied in part I.

statement:
Prove that there exists integer $n \ge 1$, such that the number of the pairs $(a, b)$ of positive integers satisfying the equation
$$
\frac{1}{a-b} - \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} = \frac{1}{n}
$$
is greater than 2024.
solution:
Choose $n=\prod_{k=1}^{2025}k(k+1)$. For each $k=1,\ldots,2025$, set
$$b_k=n+\frac{n}{k(k+1)},\qquad a_k=(k+1)b_k.$$
These are positive integers. Direct calculation gives
$$\frac1{a_k-b_k}-\frac1{a_k}+\frac1{b_k}=\frac1{b_k}\left(1+\frac1{k(k+1)}\right)=\frac1n.$$
The pairs are distinct because their ratios $a_k/b_k=k+1$ are distinct. Hence this $n$ has at least 2025 solutions.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of HELLENIC MATHEMATICAL COMPETITIONS
ratingReason: Taking a=(k+1)b parametrises a family; one must then choose a common multiple that makes more than 2024 distinct pairs integral.

statement:
If $a, b, c$ are real numbers such that two of them have difference greater than $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}$, prove that there exists an integer $x$ such that
$$
x^2 - 4(a + b + c)x + 12(ab + bc + ca) < 0.
$$
solution:
The discriminant equals to
$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta &= 16(a + b + c)^2 - 48(ab + bc + ca) \\
&= 8((a - b)^2 + (b - c)^2 + (c - a)^2).
\end{aligned}
$$
Since two of the numbers are at least $\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}$ apart, the square of their difference will be greater than $1/8$, so $\Delta > 1$. Since the discriminant is positive, the trinomial has two real roots, let $\rho_1 > \rho_2$ between which the sign of the trinomial is negative. In addition, we have:
$$
\rho_1 - \rho_2 = \frac{4(a + b + c) + \sqrt{\Delta}}{2} - \frac{4(a + b + c) - \sqrt{\Delta}}{2} = \sqrt{\Delta} > 1,
$$
so between $\rho_1, \rho_2$ there is an integer, say $x$, which makes the given trinomial negative according to the above.


Solution 2:
Consider the function
$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x) &= x^2 - 4(a + b + c)x + 12(ab + bc + ca) \\
&= x(x - 4(a + b + c)) + 12(ab + bc + ca).
\end{aligned}
$$
Observe that
$$
\begin{aligned}
f(2(a + b + c)) &= -4(a + b + c)^2 + 12(ab + bc + ca) \\
&= -2((a - b)^2 + (b - c)^2 + (c - a)^2) < 0.
\end{aligned}
$$
The graph of $f$ is a parabola, which is convex and has the vertical line $x = 2(a + b + c)$ as its axis of symmetry. Therefore
$$
f(2(a + b + c) + \frac{1}{2}) = f(2(a + b + c) - \frac{1}{2}).
$$

$$
\begin{align*}
& f(2(a+b+c) + \frac{1}{2}) \\
&= 2(a+b+c) + \frac{1}{2}(-2(a+b+c) + \frac{1}{2}) + 12(ab+bc+ca) \\
&= \frac{1}{4} - 4(a+b+c)^2 + 12(ab+bc+ca) \\
&= \frac{1}{4} - 2((a-b)^2 + (b-c)^2 + (c-a)^2) \\
&= \frac{1 - 8((a-b)^2 + (b-c)^2 + (c-a)^2)}{4} < 0,
\end{align*}
$$
since $(a-b)^2 + (b-c)^2 + (c-a)^2 > \left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{8}$. This means that the trinomial has negative sign on the interval $[2(a + b + c) - \frac{1}{2}, 2(a + b + c) + \frac{1}{2}]$, which has length 1. Therefore, there is an integer on that interval having the desired property.

ratingReason: The discriminant is eight times a sum of squared differences; showing the two roots are more than one apart gives an integer between them.

statement:
Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. We consider two finite subsets $A, B$ of the set of integers, such that the subset $A$ contains at most $n$ elements and let $\Gamma$ be a subset of the set $\{(\alpha, \beta): \alpha \in A, \beta \in B\}$. Achilles writes on a blackboard all possible differences $\alpha - \beta$, with $(\alpha, \beta) \in \Gamma$. Let $d$ be the number of all these differences. Next, Achilles writes in a second blackboard all triads $(\kappa, \lambda, \mu)$ with $(\kappa, \lambda) \in \Gamma, (\kappa, \mu) \in \Gamma$. Let $p$ be the number of all these triads. Prove that:
$$
n \cdot p \ge d^2.
$$
solution:
For the set $X$, we use the symbol $|X|$ for the number of its elements. The number of all possible differences $\alpha - \beta$, with $(\alpha, \beta) \in \Gamma$, is at most equal to the number of the elements of the set $\Gamma$, that is
$$
d \leq |\Gamma|. \qquad (*)
$$
Let $A = \{a_1, a_2, ..., a_m\}$. For each $i$, we suppose that there exist $b_i$ pairs $(a_i, b) \in \Gamma$. Then there exist $b_i^2$ triads $(a_i, \lambda, \mu)$, with $(a_i, \lambda) \in \Gamma$ and $(a_i, \mu) \in \Gamma$. Therefore, there exist totally $p = b_1^2 + \dots + b_m^2$ triads $(\kappa, \lambda, \mu)$ with $(\kappa, \lambda) \in \Gamma, (\kappa, \mu) \in \Gamma$.
From Cauchy-Schwarz inequality we get
$$
m(b_1^2 + \cdots + b_m^2) \ge (b_1 + \cdots + b_m)^2 \quad (1)
$$
The left hand side is equal to $|A| \cdot p$, while the right hand side is equal to $|\Gamma|^2$. Since it is given that $|A| \le n$, by using relations (1) and (*) we get:
$$
n \cdot p \ge |\Gamma|^2 \ge d^2.
$$
sourceName: MathNet transcription of HELLENIC MATHEMATICAL COMPETITIONS
ratingReason: Count triples as the sum of squared row sizes, then apply Cauchy-Schwarz and the immediate bound on distinct differences.

statement: Colour a $7\times7$ grid red and blue. Exactly four rows contain more blue than red cells, and exactly four columns contain more red than blue cells. What is the greatest possible side length of an axis-aligned square subgrid whose cells are all the same colour?
solution: In fact, if such a square, let $S$, existed, then each of the rows and columns of $T$ to which the sides of $S$ belong have at least $4$ squares of the same color (let with color blue in the figure $6$). This contradicts condition (ii). Therefore, for every coloring, each monochromatic square has side less or equal to $3$. The number $3$ is maximal, as we can see in figures $6$ and $7$.

statement: Determine all values of the integer $v$ for which the number $v^2 + 10v + 160$ is a perfect square.
solution:
Let $v^2 + 10v + 160 = \kappa^2$, where $\kappa$ is a positive integer. Then we have:
$$
\begin{align*}
v^2 + 10v + 160 = \kappa^2 &\Leftrightarrow (v+5)^2 + 135 = \kappa^2 \Leftrightarrow \kappa^2 - (v+5)^2 = 135 \\
&\Leftrightarrow (\kappa - |v+5|)(\kappa + |v+5|) = 135 = 1 \cdot 3^3 \cdot 5, \text{ where } \kappa > |v+5| \\
&\Leftrightarrow \begin{cases} \kappa - |v+5| = 1 \\ \kappa + |v+5| = 135 \end{cases} \text{ or } \begin{cases} \kappa - |v+5| = 3 \\ \kappa + |v+5| = 45 \end{cases} \\
&\text{or } \begin{cases} \kappa - |v+5| = 5 \\ \kappa + |v+5| = 27 \end{cases} \text{ or } \begin{cases} \kappa - |v+5| = 9 \\ \kappa + |v+5| = 15 \end{cases} \\
&\Leftrightarrow \begin{cases} \kappa = 68 \\ |v+5| = 67 \end{cases} \text{ or } \begin{cases} \kappa = 24 \\ |v+5| = 21 \end{cases} \text{ or } \begin{cases} \kappa = 16 \\ |v+5| = 11 \end{cases} \text{ or } \begin{cases} \kappa = 12 \\ |v+5| = 3 \end{cases}
\end{align*}
$$

$$
\begin{array}{l}
\Leftrightarrow \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \kappa = 68 \\ v + 5 = \pm 67 \end{array} \right\} \text{ or } \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \kappa = 24 \\ v + 5 = \pm 21 \end{array} \right\} \text{ or } \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \kappa = 16 \\ v + 5 = \pm 11 \end{array} \right\} \text{ or } \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \kappa = 12 \\ v + 5 = \pm 3 \end{array} \right\} \\[1.5ex]
\Leftrightarrow \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \kappa = 68 \\ v = 62 \ \text{or} \ v = -72 \end{array} \right\} \text{ or } \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \kappa = 24 \\ v = 16 \ \text{or} \ v = -26 \end{array} \right\} \\[1.5ex]
\text{or } \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \kappa = 16 \\ v = 6 \ \text{or} \ v = -16 \end{array} \right\} \text{ or } \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \kappa = 12 \\ v = -2 \ \text{or} \ v = -8 \end{array} \right\}.
\end{array}
$$
Therefore $v \in \{-72, -26, -16, -8, -2, 6, 16, 62\}$.

ratingReason: Completing the square leaves two factors of 135 and a short divisor enumeration.

$$
form a strictly increasing arithmetic progression in that order. Determine the smallest positive integer that could be the common difference of such an arithmetic progression.
solution:
Write $n=\nu$, the first product as $u$, and the common difference as $d>0$. Let $g=\gcd(u,d)$, and put $u=gv$, $d=gt$, where $v,t$ are coprime positive integers. For each $i=1,\ldots,n$,
$$\frac{\beta_i}{\alpha_i}=\frac{v+it}{v+(i-1)t}.$$
The numerator and denominator are coprime, so $v+(i-1)t$ divides $\alpha_i$. Multiplying gives
$$gv=u=\prod_i\alpha_i\ge\prod_{i=1}^n(v+(i-1)t),$$
so $g\ge\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}(v+it)\ge2\cdot3\cdots n=n!$. Hence $d=gt\ge n!$.

Equality is possible: choose $\alpha_i=i$ and $\beta_i=i+1$. The successive products are $n!,2n!,\ldots,(n+1)n!$, an arithmetic progression with difference $\boxed{n!}$.

statement:
A binary string is to be partitioned into blocks of two or three consecutive digits. The partition is valid if either every block is nondecreasing, or every block is nonincreasing.

(a) Prove that a string consisting of $m$ zeros followed by $n$ ones, with $m+n\ge2$, admits a valid partition.

(b) For $\ell\ge4$, prove that exactly $2^{\ell-3}$ binary strings of length $\ell$ admit no valid partition.
solution:
(a) Any length at least 2 is a sum of 2s and 3s; every resulting block is nondecreasing.

(b) A nondecreasing-block partition is impossible if the string begins with 10 or ends with 10, since the first or last block would contain that descent. Conversely, if neither happens, split at every occurrence of 10. Each resulting substring is nondecreasing and has length at least 2: an interior substring contains both digits, and the two endpoint substrings are not singletons by the endpoint assumptions. Part (a) partitions them as required.

Similarly a nonincreasing-block partition exists exactly when the string neither begins nor ends with 01. Thus both kinds fail exactly for strings beginning 01 and ending 10, or beginning 10 and ending 01. Each class has $2^{\ell-4}$ members, yielding $2^{\ell-3}$.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of Olimpiadi di Matematica
ratingReason: The count comes only after characterising failure by the two endpoint pairs; the existence proof partitions into maximal monotone runs.
notes: The endpoint condition is stated explicitly to avoid a reversed initial digit in the transcription.

section: District round (21 February 2024) — Problemi a risposta multipla
statement:
Qual è la somma dei divisori positivi di $18000$ la cui scrittura decimale termina per $50$?

(A) $1400$
(B) $1650$
(C) $3150$
(D) $3900$
(E) $4030$
solution:
La risposta è $(\mathbf{D})$. Si ha che $18000=2^{4} \cdot 3^{2} \cdot 5^{3}$, quindi tutti i divisori di $18000$ sono del tipo $2^{a} \cdot 3^{b} \cdot 5^{c}$, dove $a \in\{0,1,2,3,4\}$, $b \in\{0,1,2\}$ e $c \in\{0,1,2,3\}$. Affinché la scrittura decimale del divisore termini con $50$, il numero deve essere divisibile per $50$, da cui $a \geq 1$ e $c \geq 2$. Notiamo, inoltre, che se $a \geq 2$ e $c \geq 2$, allora la scrittura decimale del divisore termina con le cifre "00". È quindi necessario richiedere anche $a=1$. Quindi la somma richiesta è data da
$$
\sum_{b=0}^{2} \sum_{c=2}^{3} 2 \cdot 3^{b} \cdot 5^{c} = 2 \cdot \left(\sum_{b=0}^{2} 3^{b}\right) \cdot \left(\sum_{c=2}^{3} 5^{c}\right) = 2 \cdot 13 \cdot 150 = 3900.
$$
sourceName: MathNet transcription of Italian Mathematical Olympiad - February Round
ratingReason: Ending in 50 fixes the exponent of 2 and bounds the exponent of 5, leaving a short product of geometric sums.

section: District round (21 February 2024) — Problemi a risposta multipla
statement:
Determinare il numero di coppie $(m, n)$ di numeri interi di modulo minore di $10000$ che risolvono l'equazione $n^{2}+2024 n+2024 m=2024$.

(A) 4
(B) 9
(C) 10
(D) 18
(E) 19
solution:
La risposta è (B). Innanzitutto notiamo che $2024=2^{3} \cdot 11 \cdot 23$ deve dividere $n^{2}$, quindi possiamo scrivere $n=\left(2^{2} \cdot 11 \cdot 23\right) \cdot k=1012 k$, con $k$ intero di modulo minore o uguale a $9$, così che $|n|=|1012 k|<10000$. Sostituendo nell'equazione abbiamo
$$
1012^{2} k^{2}+2 \cdot 1012^{2} k+2024 m=2024,
$$
e dividendo per $2024$ si ha
$$
506 k^{2}+1012 k-1=-m.
$$
Il numero di soluzioni $(n, m)$ è dunque pari al numero di interi $-10<k<10$ tali che
$$
-10000<506 k^{2}+1012 k-1<10000 ;
$$
infatti, una volta scelto $k$, l'intero $m$ è univocamente determinato. Si osserva facilmente che per $k \leq -6$ o $k \geq 4$ la disuguaglianza non è verificata, mentre lo è per tutti gli interi tra $-5$ e $3$, che sono $9$.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of Olimpiadi di Matematica
ratingReason: Divisibility forces n=1012k; substitution leaves a small bounded quadratic count.

section: District round (21 February 2024) — Problemi a risposta numerica
statement: A truncated cube has six regular octagonal faces and eight equilateral triangular faces. Label its faces with $1,\ldots,14$, once each, so that opposite faces always have the same sum. How many different labellings are there, counting two as the same when a rotation takes one to the other?
solution:
There are seven opposite-face pairs. Their common sum must be $105/7=15$, so the numerical pairs are $(1,14),(2,13),\ldots,(7,8)$. Assign them to the seven geometric pairs in $7!$ ways, and choose each pair's orientation in $2^7$ ways.

The truncated cube has 24 rotational symmetries: choose which of six octagonal faces goes on the bottom, then one of four rotations about the vertical axis. Every orbit of a labelling has exactly 24 members, since distinct labels prevent a nonidentity rotation from fixing it. Hence the required number is $2^7\cdot7!/24=\boxed{26880}$.

ratingReason: The count combines assignment of seven complementary face-pairs with the 24 rotations of a cube; one must justify that the rotation action has no stabilisers.

section: District round (21 February 2024) — Problemi a risposta multipla
statement:
Alberto ha davanti a sé 13 caselle disposte una sopra l'altra, e vuole inserirvi i numeri da 1 a 10, uno per casella (tre caselle rimarranno vuote). Vuole inoltre che, se due numeri sono scritti in caselle che si toccano, quello più in alto sia maggiore. In quanti modi può farlo?

(A) $3^{10}$
(B) $2^{11} \cdot 3^{3} \cdot 13$
(C) $2^{16} \cdot 13$
(D) $2^{20}$
(E) $2^{9} \cdot 3^{4} \cdot 5^{2} \cdot 7 \cdot 11 \cdot 13$
solution: La risposta è (D). Le quattro caselle lasciate bianche partizionano i 10 numeri in quattro sottoinsiemi (eventualmente vuoti). All'interno di ciascuno di questi sottoinsiemi, l'ordine dei numeri inseriti nelle caselle è determinato. Poiché ciascuno dei 10 numeri può finire in uno qualsiasi dei quattro insiemi, l'insieme delle disposizioni possibili è $4^{10} = 2^{20}$.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of Italian Mathematical Olympiad - February Round
ratingReason: The three empty cells split the numbers into four ordered blocks; assigning each number to its block determines the internal order.

section: District round (21 February 2024) — Problemi a risposta multipla
statement:
Sono dati, nello spazio, tre punti distinti $X, Y$ e $Z$; ci si chiede se esista un punto $P$ diverso da $X, Y$ e $Z$ tale che le rette $P X, P Y$ e $P Z$ siano a due a due perpendicolari. Quattro amici fanno le seguenti affermazioni:

Alberto: "Esistono $X, Y, Z$ e $P$ appartenenti allo stesso piano che soddisfano tali condizioni."

Barbara: "Non esistono 4 punti $X, Y, Z$ e $P$ che soddisfano tali condizioni."

Carlo: "Affinché $P$ esista è necessario che $X Y Z$ sia acutangolo."

Daria: "Affinché $P$ esista è sufficiente che $X Y Z$ non sia ottusangolo."

Chi ha ragione?

(A) Solo Alberto
(B) Solo Barbara
(C) Solo Carlo
(D) Solo Daria
(E) Nessuna delle precedenti.
solution:
La risposta è $(\mathbf{C})$. L'unico che ha ragione è Carlo.

Alberto ha torto, infatti se esistessero $X, Y, Z, P$ appartenenti allo stesso piano tali che $P X, P Y$ e $P Z$ sono a due a due perpendicolari allora $P Z \perp P X, P Z \perp P Y$ e quindi $P Y \parallel P X$, che è assurdo.

Barbara ha torto: 4 punti siffatti sono ad esempio dati dagli estremi di 3 spigoli di un cubo aventi un vertice in comune (che sarà $P$), o più in generale dai vertici di un qualsiasi tetraedro rettangolo.

Carlo ha ragione: infatti dato che $X Y^{2} = P X^{2} + P Y^{2} < P X^{2} + P Y^{2} + 2 \cdot P Z^{2} = X Z^{2} + Y Z^{2}$, allora $\widehat{X Z Y}$ è acuto, e analogamente anche $\widehat{Z X Y}$ e $\widehat{X Y Z}$ sono acuti. Un'argomentazione alternativa per mostrare che Carlo ha ragione è la seguente: consideriamo la sfera di diametro $X Y$, allora $P$ appartiene a tale sfera e la retta $P Z$ è la perpendicolare al piano su cui giacciono $P, X, Y$, dunque ogni punto di tale retta (fatta eccezione per $P$) è esterno alla sfera. Ma allora $\widehat{X Z Y}$ è acuto (e analogamente anche $\widehat{Z X Y}$ e $\widehat{X Y Z}$ sono acuti).

Daria ha torto: per quanto detto sopra, è necessario che $X Y Z$ sia acutangolo, quindi $X Y Z$ non può essere rettangolo; in particolare, non è sufficiente che $X Y Z$ non sia ottusangolo.

ratingReason: Pairwise perpendicular edges give three Pythagorean identities, immediately forcing all base angles to be acute.

statement:
Diciamo che una coppia $(a, b)$ di interi positivi è bella se $a$ divide $b$ e $a+1$ divide $b+1$.

a. Dimostrare che, fissato un intero positivo $a$, esistono infiniti interi positivi $b$ tali che la coppia $(a, b)$ sia bella.

b. Fissato un intero positivo $a$, determinare il minimo intero $b>a$ tale che $(a, b)$ sia bella.

c. Preso ora $a=18$, determinare il minimo intero positivo $b>a$ tale che $(a, b)$ sia bella ed inoltre $a+2$ divida $b+2$.
solution:
Per definizione, una coppia di interi positivi $(a, b)$ è bella se esistono $k, h$ interi positivi tali che $b=k a$ e $b+1=h(a+1)$. In particolare, si ha $k a+1=h(a+1)$ e quindi
$$
h=\frac{k a+1}{a+1} .
$$
Poiché $h$ è intero, si ha che $k a+1=k(a+1)-(k-1)$ è divisibile per $a+1$, da cui $k-1$ è divisibile per $a+1$ e quindi esiste $n$ intero non negativo tale per cui $k-1=n(a+1)$. Mettendo tutto insieme, otteniamo che se la coppia $(a, b)$ è bella allora esiste un intero $n$ per cui $b=k a=a(n a+n+1)$.
D'altra parte, se $b=a(n a+n+1)$ per qualche intero non negativo $n$, allora, chiaramente, $a$ divide $b$ e $b+1=(n a+n+1) a+1=n(a+1) a+(a+1)$ è divisibile per $a+1$.
Riassumendo, la coppia $(a, b)$ è bella se e solo se $b=a(n a+n+1)$ per qualche intero positivo $n$.

a. Dato $a$, esistono infiniti interi positivi $b$ per cui la coppia $(a, b)$ è bella: infatti, segue da quando detto sopra che per ogni intero positivo $n$ la coppia $(a, a(n a+n+1))$ è bella.

Seconda soluzione: per ogni $d$ intero positivo dispari, la coppia del tipo $(a, a^{d})$ è bella: chiaramente $a$ divide $a^{d}$; inoltre $a^{d}+1=(a+1)(1-a+a^{2}-a^{3}+\ldots+a^{d-1})$ è divisibile per $a+1$. Abbiamo così ottenuto un'altra famiglia infinita di coppie belle $(a, b)$ con $a$ dato.

b. Si osservi che, se $m>n$, allora $a(m a+m+1)>a(n a+n+1)$. Poiché le coppie belle sono tutte e sole del tipo $(a, a(n a+n+1))$ (per $n$ intero non negativo) e poiché per $n=0$ si ha $a(n a+n+1)=a$, il minimo intero $b>a$ per cui $(a, b)$ sia bella si ottiene per $n=1$, cioè $b=a^{2}+2 a>a$.

Seconda soluzione: Dato $a$, il minimo $b$ (tale per cui $b>a$ e $(a, b)$ è una coppia bella) è un multiplo di $a$ del tipo $m a$ ($m>1$ intero). Osservo che se $m a+1$ da come resto $r$ nella divisione per $a+1$, allora $(m+1) a+1=(m a+1)+(a+1)-1$ da come resto $r-1$. Poiché per $m=1$ il resto della divisione di $m a+1$ per $a+1$ è nullo, il multiplo successivo di $a$ ad avere tale proprietà sarà dato quando $m=a+2$, cioè $b=(a+2) a$.

c. Da quanto detto sopra, sappiamo che la coppia $(18, b)$ è bella se e solo se $b=18(18 n+n+1)=18(19 n+1)$. La condizione
$$
20=a+2 \mid b+2=342 n+20,
$$
è soddisfatta se e solo se 20 divide $342 n$ o, equivalentemente, se 10 divide $n$. Deduciamo così che il minimo $b=18(19 n+1)$ maggiore di 18 per cui la coppia $(18, b)$ è bella e $b+2$ divide $a+2=20$ si ottiene per $n=10$, ovvero $b=191 \cdot 18=3438$.

ratingReason: All conditions say that b-a is divisible by consecutive integers; the minimum follows from a small lcm.
