statement: We will call a natural number $m$ remarkable if there exist integers $a$, $b$, $c$, for which $m = a^3 + 2b^3 + 4c^3 - 6abc$. Prove that there exists a natural number $n < 2024$ such that for infinitely many prime numbers $p$, the number $np$ is remarkable.
solution:
Lemma. Let $p$ be a prime number and $a$, $b$, $c \in \mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$. Then there exist $x$, $y$, $z \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $|x|$, $|y|$, $|z| < \sqrt[3]{p}$, $(x, y, z) \neq (0, 0, 0)$ and $ax + by + cz \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$.

*Proof.* Consider the set $M := \{(x, y, z) : x, y, z \in \{0, 1, \dots, \lfloor \sqrt[3]{p} \rfloor\}\}$. We have that $|M| > p$, i.e. in $M$ there are two distinct elements $(x_1, y_1, z_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2, z_2)$, for which $ax_1 + by_1 + cz_1 \equiv ax_2 + by_2 + cz_2 \pmod{p}$. Thus $(x_1 - x_2, y_1 - y_2, z_1 - z_2)$ satisfies the conditions of the lemma.

Now let $p \equiv 2 \pmod{3}$. Then the comparison $x^3 \equiv 2 \pmod{p}$ has a solution $a$, since the function $x \mapsto x^3$ is injective in $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$, hence it is surjective. One way to verify this is to see that $x^3 \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$ has only $1$ for a solution, since $(3, p-1) = 1$ and hence the exponent of $x$ (mod $p$) is $1$.

From the lemma, there exist $x$, $y$, $z$ with $|x|$, $|y|$, $|z| < \sqrt[3]{p}$, for which $x + ay + a^2z \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$. From here we get that $x^3 + a^3y^3 + a^6z^3 - 3a^3xyz \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$. The latter is equivalent to $x^3 + 2y^3 + 4z^3 - 6xyz \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$.

On the other hand $|x|$, $|y|$, $|z| < \sqrt[3]{p}$ gives $|x^3 + 2y^3 + 4z^3 - 6xyz| < 13p$. Also notice that if $x^3 + 2y^3 + 4z^3 - 6xyz < 0$, then the triple $(-x, -y, -z)$ will give a natural number divisible by $p$.

It remains to note that $x^3 + 2y^3 + 4z^3 - 6xyz \neq 0$. Indeed, if $x^3 + 2y^3 + 4z^3 - 6xyz = 0$, then we have $(x + \sqrt[3]{2}y + \sqrt[3]{4}z)((x - \sqrt[3]{2}y)^2 + (x - \sqrt[3]{4}z)^2 + (\sqrt[3]{2}y - \sqrt[3]{4}z)^2) = 0$, i.e. $x = \sqrt[3]{2}y = \sqrt[3]{4}z$ or $x + y\sqrt[3]{2} + z\sqrt[3]{4} = 0$, whose only integer solutions are $(x, y, z) = (0, 0, 0)$ (the first follows because $\sqrt[3]{2}$ is irrational, and the second follows from the fact that $x^3 - 2$ is the minimal polynomial of $\sqrt[3]{2}$ over the rational numbers). $\square$
sourceName: MathNet transcription of Bulgarian Competitions 2023-2024
ratingReason: Combine small modular kernel vectors, a cubic norm, irreducibility and infinitely many primes in a residue class.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - First Day - 8th Grade
statement:
Oleksii placed positive integers in the cells of the chessboard of size $8 \times 8$. For each pair of adjacent cells, Fedir wrote down the product of the numbers in them and added all the obtained numbers. Oleksii wrote down the sum of the numbers in each pair of adjacent cells and multiplied all the obtained numbers. It turned out that both numbers have the same last digit, $1$. Prove that at least one of the boys made a mistake in the calculation. For example, for the square $3 \times 3$ and the given arrangement of numbers (fig. 11), Fedir would write the following numbers: $2$, $6$, $8$, $24$, $15$, $35$, $2$, $6$, $8$, $20$, $18$, $42$ and their sum ends with digit $6$, and Oleksii would write the following numbers: $3$, $5$, $6$, $10$, $8$, $12$, $3$, $5$, $6$, $9$, $9$, $13$ and their product ends with digit $0$.

(Oleksii Masalitin, Fedir Yudin)

| 1 | 2 | 3 |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 4 | 6 |
| 3 | 5 | 7 |

Fig. 11
solution: Suppose that this could happen. Since Oleksii's product is odd, all the factors are odd, and therefore the sum of the numbers in any neighboring cells is odd. But then for any neighboring cells, the parity of the numbers in those cells is different, and therefore the product of those numbers is even, and therefore the sum is even. Contradiction.

ratingReason: An odd product of edge sums forces every edge product even, so their total cannot be odd.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - First Day - 8th Grade
statement:
A country held a one-round tennis tournament. Participants received $1$ point for winning the match, and $0$ points for losing. There are no draws in tennis. At the end of the tournament, Oleksii saw the number of points scored by each participant, as well as the schedule of all the matches in the tournament, which showed the pairs of players, but not the winners. He chooses a match in some particular order (however he wants) and tries to guess the winner, after which he is told if he is correct. Prove that Oleksii can act in such a way that he is guaranteed to guess the winners of more than half of the matches.
(Oleksii Masalitin)
solution: Let's choose player $A$, who has the lowest number of points. He has at least as many defeats as wins, so by indicating a defeat in each his game, Oleksii will guess at least half of the results of player $A$. Then Oleksii subtracts the results of player $A$ from the results of each participant and again selects player $B$ with the lowest number of points and repeats this procedure. If the corresponding player has an odd number of games, then Oleksii will guess more than half of the results of this player, if the number of games is even, then at least half, but then he guessed more than half for $A$ and $B$ together, since the number of games for them was of different parity. Let's continue to choose the player with the lowest number of points. In total, he will guess more than half of all outcomes.

ratingReason: Repeatedly predict losses for a minimum-score player; odd residual degrees give strict improvement.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - First Day - 8th Grade
statement:
The positive integers $x$, $y$ satisfy the conditions:
$$
\{\sqrt{x^2 + 2y}\} > \frac{2}{3}, \{\sqrt{y^2 + 2x}\} > \frac{2}{3}.
$$
Prove that $x = y$.
Here, $\{a\} \in [0; 1)$ denotes the fractional part of the number $a$, that is, there exists an integer $n$ for which the equality $a = n + \{a\}$ holds. For example, $\{3.14\} = 0.14$.
solution:
Suppose $x<y$. Then $y<\sqrt{y^2+2x}<y+1$, so the second condition gives $x>2y/3$. Since $y\ge x+1$, the first radical is larger than $x+1$. Since $2y<3x<4x+4$, it is smaller than $x+2$. Thus the first condition gives
$$x^2+2y>(x+5/3)^2,$$
so $y>5x/3$. Combining yields $x>10x/9$, impossible. Interchanging $x,y$ handles the other unequal ordering.

ratingReason: Pin down the integer parts and obtain incompatible bounds on the ratio x/y.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - First Day - 8th Grade
statement: In rhombus $ABCD$, a point $T$ satisfies $\angle ATC+\angle BTD=180^\circ$, and circles $ATC$ and $BTD$ are tangent. Prove that $T$ has equal distances from the two diagonal lines.
solution:
Let $P$ be the point of intersection of the rhombus diagonals, $O_1$ and $O_2$ be the centers of the described circles $\Delta ATC$ and $\Delta BTD$ respectively. Hence, the following equalities are true:
$$
\angle A O_1 C = 2 \angle A T C = 2 \cdot (180^\circ - \angle B T D) = \angle B O_2 D,
$$
so the isosceles triangles $AO_1C$ and $BO_2D$ are similar. Then their altitudes are proportional to their sides, i.e. $\frac{PO_1}{PO_2} = \frac{O_1A}{O_2B} = \frac{O_1T}{O_2T}$. Then $PT$ is a bisector (internal or external) of $\angle O_1PO_2$, exactly what we needed to prove.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of UKRAINIAN MATHEMATICAL COMPETITIONS
ratingReason: The central-angle relation gives a radius ratio; tangency turns it into an angle-bisector condition.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - Second Day - 9th grade
statement: Are there any 10 numbers, not all of which are the same, each of which is equal to the square of the sum of all the other numbers?
solution:
Suppose that such numbers exist. Since they are equal to some squares, each of these numbers is nonnegative. Let's denote the sum of all these 10 numbers by $S$. Let's pick one of these numbers and denote it by $a$, then $S \ge a$, and also
$$
a = (S - a)^2 \Rightarrow a^2 - (2S + 1)a + S^2 = 0.
$$
If there are two different $a$, satisfying this condition, then by Vieta's theorem their product is equal to $S^2$. However, this means that one of them is greater than $S$, which contradicts what we proved above. Thus, there is only one possible $a$, and it follows that all numbers are equal.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of UKRAINIAN MATHEMATICAL COMPETITIONS
ratingReason: All entries are nonnegative; a+sqrt(a)=S is strictly increasing, so every entry must coincide.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - Second Day - 10th grade
statement: In a convex pentagon $ABCDE$, suppose $AB\parallel CD$, $BC\parallel DE$ and $\angle BAE=\angle AED$. Show that $AB+BC=CD+DE$.
solution:
Let the rays $AB$ and $DE$ intersect at the point $O$ (fig. 16). Then $BCDO$ is a parallelogram, and $\Delta AOE$ is isosceles, since $\angle OAE = \angle AEO$. So,
$$
AB + BC = (OB - OA) + BC = CD - OE + OD = CD + DE.
$$

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - Second Day - 8th Grade
statement: An undirected flight network has $n\ge3$ airports. Each day, close the airport whose number of flights is strictly greater than that of every other remaining airport, and remove its flights. If there is no such airport, stop. Over all starting networks, what is the maximum number of days?
solution:
Pass to the complementary graph: at each step delete its unique vertex of minimum degree. With two vertices this is impossible. If four vertices $A,B,C,D$ remain and $D$ can be deleted, then it is impossible to delete $C$ next. Indeed, in a three-vertex graph a unique minimum-degree vertex must be isolated while the other two are adjacent. Thus $C$ has degree at most one before $D$ is deleted. For $D$ to have strictly smaller degree it must have degree zero, leaving $C$ also with degree zero, a contradiction.
For $n\ge4$, at least three vertices therefore remain. Equality is achieved by the complement consisting of the path $A_1A_2\cdots A_n$ with the additional edge $A_{n-2}A_n$: successive unique leaves $A_1,\ldots,A_{n-3}$ can be deleted, leaving a triangle. Hence the maximum is $n-3$.
For $n=3$, take a complementary graph with one edge and one isolated vertex. Exactly one deletion is possible, so the maximum is $1$.

ratingReason: A four-vertex obstruction gives the upper bound, and a path ending in a triangle attains it.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - Second Day - 8th Grade
statement: You are given a set of $m$ positive integers such that they all give distinct remainders modulo some positive integer $n$. Prove that for any positive integer $k \leq m$ this set can be partitioned into $k$ nonempty subsets such that the sums of the numbers in these subsets are also distinct modulo $n$.
solution:
Let these numbers be $a_1, a_2, ..., a_m$. It is enough to show that you can choose some two of these numbers $a_i, a_j$ (with $i < j$) so that all the numbers $a_1, a_2, ..., a_{i-1}, a_{i+1}, ..., a_{j-1}, a_{j+1}, ..., a_m, a_i + a_j$ give distinct remainders when divided by $n$, then we can combine the numbers $(m-k)$ times and get the statement of the problem.
If any of the numbers is divisible by $n$, for example, $a_1$ then we can combine the numbers $a_1, a_2$.
Otherwise, replace these numbers with their remainders when divided by $n$ and sort them. Let $0 < a_1 < a_2 ... < a_m < n$. Then we can combine $a_1, a_m$. Indeed: for any $j$, $a_1 + a_m > a_j$ and $a_1 + a_m < a_j + n$, so this remainder does not occur among the others.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of UKRAINIAN MATHEMATICAL COMPETITIONS
ratingReason: Merging a zero residue, or the smallest and largest nonzero residues, preserves distinctness.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - First Day - 9th grade
statement: $n \ge 4$ real numbers are placed on the circle. It is known that for any four consecutive numbers $a, b, c, d$ that go around the circle in this specified order, the condition $a + d = b + c$ holds. For which $n$ can we conclude that all the numbers are equal?
solution:
We denote the numbers in the circle by $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$. Choose the largest among them (or any of them, if there are several such numbers). Without loss of generality, let this number be $a_1$. From the condition of the problem we have that
$$
a_1 + a_2 = a_n + a_3, \quad a_1 + a_n = a_2 + a_{n-1} \Rightarrow 2a_1 = a_3 + a_{n-1}.
$$
Since $a_1$ is the largest number, the last equality implies that $a_1 = a_3 = a_{n-1}$: that is, every second number is the largest, if we continue with the same reasoning. If $n$ is odd, then all the numbers will be equal.

For even numbers $n$ it is enough to consider the following example with not all equal numbers: $1, 0, 1, 0, \ldots, 1, 0$.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of UKRAINIAN MATHEMATICAL COMPETITIONS
ratingReason: A maximum propagates two positions at a time; alternating values handle even n.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - First Day - 9th grade
statement: Positive integers $a_1, a_2, ..., a_{101}$ are such that $a_i + 1$ are divisible by $a_{i+1}$ for $1 \le i \le 101$ (we assume that $a_{102} = a_1$). What is the largest value that the maximum of these numbers can attain?
solution: Without loss of generality, let $a_{101}$ be the largest of these numbers (or one of the largest). It is clear that $a_i + 1 \ge a_{i+1}$ for any $i = 1, 100$. If we add all these 100 inequalities, we get $a_1 + a_2 + ... + a_{100} + 100 \ge a_2 + a_3 + ... + a_{101}$, that is $a_1 \ge a_{101} - 100$. From the condition $a_{101} + 1$ is divisible by $a_1$, and from the fact that $a_{101}$ is the largest we have $a_{101} + 1 > a_1$, so $a_{101} + 1 \ge 2a_1 \ge 2(a_{101} - 100) = 2a_{101} - 200$, therefore $a_{101} \le 201$. It remains to show that there is an example where the maximum is equal to 201. Indeed, consider the set 101, 102, ..., 201, for it $a_i + 1 = a_{i+1}$ for $i = 1, 100$ and $a_{101} + 1 = 2a_1$, so this example satisfies the problem.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of UKRAINIAN MATHEMATICAL COMPETITIONS
ratingReason: Sum the successor bounds around the cycle and exploit the final strict multiple; consecutive values attain the bound.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - First Day - 9th grade
statement: Find the least real $C$ such that, for all distinct positive integers $x,y$, $$\min\bigl(\{\sqrt{x^2+2y}\},\{\sqrt{y^2+2x}\}\bigr)<C,$$ where $\{t\}=t-\lfloor t\rfloor$.
solution:
Put $c=(\sqrt5-1)/2$, so $c(c+1)=1$. Suppose $x<y$ and both fractional parts are at least $c$. Since $y<\sqrt{y^2+2x}<y+1$, we obtain $2x\ge2cy+c^2$, hence $x>cy$. Also $y\ge x+1$, while $2y<2x/c<4x$, so
$$x+1<\sqrt{x^2+2y}<x+2.$$
The first fractional-part condition now yields $2y\ge2(c+1)x+(c+1)^2$, hence $y>(c+1)x$. Multiplication contradicts $c(c+1)=1$. Thus the minimum is always strictly below $c$.
To prove sharpness, let $x$ tend through positive integers and put $y=\lfloor(c+1)x\rfloor$. For sufficiently large $x$, the two radicals lie between $x+1,x+2$ and $y,y+1$, respectively. Rationalizing shows
$$\sqrt{x^2+2y}-x\longrightarrow c+1,\qquad\sqrt{y^2+2x}-y\longrightarrow\frac1{c+1}=c.$$
Their fractional parts both tend to $c$. No smaller constant works, so the answer is $c$.

ratingReason: The golden-ratio bound needs both an integer-part argument and an asymptotic extremal construction.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - Second Day - 9th grade
statement: Inside triangle $ABC$, let $O$ satisfy $\angle BOC=90^\circ-\angle BAC$. Rays $BO,CO$ meet $AC,AB$ at $K,L$. Choose $K_1\in LC$, $L_1\in BK$ with $BK_1=K_1K$ and $CL_1=L_1L$. If $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$, prove $\angle K_1ML_1=90^\circ$.
solution:
Let $K_2$ and $L_2$ be the midpoints of the segments $BK$ and $CL$ respectively (fig. 18). Then $MK_2 \parallel AC$ and $ML_2 \parallel AB$. Hence, $\angle K_2ML_2 = \angle BAC$. From the isosceles triangles $BK_1K$ and $CL_1L$ we have that $\angle L_1L_2K_1 = \angle K_1K_2L_1 = 90^\circ$ and then $L_1, L_2, K_1, K_2$ lie on the same circle with diameter $K_1L_1$. Also note that
$$ \angle K_2K_1L_2 = \angle K_2L_1L_2 = 90^\circ - \angle BOC = \angle BAC = \angle K_2ML_2. $$
So, $M$ also lies on a circle with diameter $K_1L_1$. Hence, $\angle K_1ML_1 = 90^\circ$.

ratingReason: Introduce two segment midpoints and prove that all five relevant points lie on one diameter circle.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - Second Day - 9th grade
statement:
You are given $n \ge 2$ distinct positive integers. A pair of integers is called *elegant* if their sum is $2^k$ for some positive integer $k$. For each $n$ find the largest possible number of *elegant* pairs.
(Oleksii Masalitin)
solution:
**Answer:** $n-1$

We prove that there exist at most $n-1$ *elegant* pairs by induction by $n$. The base case for $n=2$ is obvious, we prove the transition. Let the statement be proved for $n-1$, let us prove it for $n$ numbers. Let us denote by $a$ the largest of them, suppose that the number $a$ is contained in some two *elegant* pairs. Then $a+b$ and $a+c$ are powers of two. Let us denote by $m$ a number such that $2^m \le a < 2^{m+1}$. Then $a+b$ and $a+c$ are greater than $2^m$, but less than $2a < 2^{m+2}$, because $a+b = a+c = 2^{m+1}$, which contradicts the fact that the numbers are pairwise distinct. By induction, among other $n-1$ integers there are no more than $n-2$ *elegant* pairs, so there are no more than $n-1$ in total, which completes the proof of the transition.

It remains to show that there can be $n-1$ *elegant* pairs for any $n \ge 2$. Indeed, let us choose $a_1 = 1$, $a_2 = 2^2-1$, $a_3 = 2^3-1$, $\ldots$, $a_n = 2^n-1$. Then the pairs $(a_1, a_i)$ are elegant for $i = \underline{2, n}$.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of UKRAINIAN MATHEMATICAL COMPETITIONS
ratingReason: The largest number belongs to at most one power-of-two pair; induction and a star construction give n−1.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - Second Day - 9th grade
statement: What is the maximum possible number of edges in a graph with $2n$ vertices, if there is exactly one way to divide its vertices into $n$ pairs such that in each pair the vertices are connected by an edge?
solution:
Consider this partition into pairs, denote the vertices $A_1, A_2, ..., A_{2n}$ where the vertices $A_{2i-1}, A_{2i}$ are connected by an edge for each $i$ from $1$ to $n$. Note that for every two pairs $(A_{2i-1}, A_{2i})$, $(A_{2j-1}, A_{2j})$, there are at most two edges between them: there cannot be two edges $(A_{2i-1}, A_{2j-1})$, $(A_{2i}, A_{2j})$, as then we could replace the chosen edges with these and still get a perfect pairing, and also the edges $(A_{2i-1}, A_{2j})$, $(A_{2i}, A_{2j-1})$. Thus, there can be no more than $n + 2 \cdot C_n^2 = n^2$ edges in total.

The example looks like this: we draw all the edges of the form $(A_{2i-1}, A_{2i})$, and also for each $i < j$ draw the edges $(A_{2i-1}, A_{2j-1})$, $(A_{2i-1}, A_{2j})$. Consider any perfect pairing in this graph. Notice that the vertex $A_2$ is connected only to $A_1$ so it must have an edge $(A_1, A_2)$. Among the remaining vertices, the vertex $A_4$ is connected only to $A_3$ so there must be an edge in the pairing $(A_3, A_4)$. Continuing similarly, all edges $(A_{2i-1}, A_{2i})$ will be in this pairing.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of UKRAINIAN MATHEMATICAL COMPETITIONS
ratingReason: Each pair of matching edges allows at most two cross-edges; a triangular construction has a forced matching.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - First Day - 10th grade
statement: Given a positive integer $k$. The product of some $k$ consecutive positive integers ends with the number $k$. What value can the number $k$ attain?
solution: If $k\ge5$, every product of $k$ consecutive positive integers is divisible by $10$, so its suffix $k$ must be divisible by $10$. Thus $k\ge10$. Such a product is divisible by $k!$, because it equals $k!\binom{a+k-1}{k}$ for some positive $a$. Since $(k-1)!$ is divisible by $10$, the product is divisible by $10k$. It therefore has strictly more trailing zeroes than $k$, contradicting the suffix condition. Hence $k\le4$. For $k=3$ the product is even and cannot end in 3. The values $1,2,4$ occur in $1$, $1\cdot2$, and $1\cdot2\cdot3\cdot4=24$.

ratingReason: Trailing-zero divisibility eliminates large suffixes; small cases must then be checked.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - First Day - 10th grade
statement: On a rectangular board $100 \times 300$ two people take turns coloring the uncolored cells. The first one paints yellow, the second one paints blue. The coloring is completed when every cell on the board is colored. A *sequence of* cells is a set of cells in which two consecutive cells share a common side (all cells in the sequence are different). Consider all possible sequences of yellow cells. The *result* of the first player is the number of cells in the sequence of yellow cells of maximum length. The first player's goal is to maximize the result, and the second player's goal is to make the first player's result as small as possible. Prove that if each player strives to achieve his goal, the first player's result will be no more than $200$.
solution: Let's divide the entire board into vertical dominoes, whose larger sides are parallel to the larger side of the board. Let's consider the second player's strategy: he paints the second square of the domino whose first square was painted by the first player in the previous move. Then it is clear that no sequence of yellow cells crosses the horizontal grid lines of the rectangular board, which divide the dominoes in half. So under such conditions, the sequence with the maximum number of yellow cells can contain only the adjacent two rows of our board, that is, its result will not exceed $200$, which is what we needed to prove.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of UKRAINIAN MATHEMATICAL COMPETITIONS
ratingReason: Pair cells to create impassable lines, limiting every yellow path to a two-row strip.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - First Day - 10th grade
statement:
Let $(x_n)$ be a sequence of real numbers from the interval $(0; 1)$. The sequence of positive integers $(a_n)$ is defined as follows: $a_1 = 1$, $a_{i+1} = m$, where $m$ is the smallest positive integer for which $[x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_m] = a_i$. Prove that for any indexes $i, j$ the inequality $a_{i+j} \ge a_i + a_j$ holds.
(Nazar Serdyuk)
solution:
Note that we can put $a_0 = 0$, then we would get $a_1 = 1$. First, let's prove the following lemma:

**Lemma.** For all $i \in \mathbb{N}$ the condition holds: $a_{i+1} - a_i \ge a_i - a_{i-1}$.

*Proof:*
$$
x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_{2a_i - a_{i-1} - 1} = (x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_{a_i}) + (x_{a_i + 1} + x_{a_i + 2} + \cdots + x_{2a_i - a_{i-1} - 1}) < \\
< (a_{i-1} + 1) + (1 + 1 + \cdots + 1)_{\text{($a_i - a_{i-1} - 1$ terms)}} < (a_{i-1} + 1) + (a_i - a_{i-1} - 1) = a_i.
$$
Thus, $a_{i+1}$ there must be at least $2a_i - a_{i-1}$.

Let's choose some positive integer $t$. First, write down the inequalities of the form $a_{i-k} - a_{i-k-1} \ge a_{i-k-1} - a_{i-k-2}$, $k = 0, \ldots, t-1$.
Add up all these inequalities: $a_i - a_{i-t} \ge a_{i-1} - a_{i-t-1}$ and then we have that
$$
a_i - a_{i-t} \ge a_{i-1} - a_{i-t-1} \ge a_{i-2} - a_{i-t-2} \ge \cdots \ge a_t - a_0.
$$
Now we just put $i \to i+j$, $t \to j$ and get the desired inequality from the problem: $a_{i+j} \ge a_i + a_j$.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of UKRAINIAN MATHEMATICAL COMPETITIONS
ratingReason: Show successive differences are nondecreasing by exploiting minimal crossing indices, then telescope.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - Second Day - 10th grade
statement: Let $P(x)$, $Q(x)$ and $R(x)$ be polynomials with integer coefficients, such that the equality holds: $P(x) = Q(x)R(x)$. We denote by $a$ and $b$ the maximum of the absolute values of coefficients of the polynomials $P(x)$ and $Q(x)$ respectively. Does the condition $b \le 2023a$ always hold?
solution:
**Answer:** No, not necessarily.

As an example, consider the following two polynomials:

$$
Q(x) = 1 + 2x + 3x^2 + 4x^3 + \cdots + 2023x^{2022} + 2024x^{2023} + 2023x^{2024} + \cdots + x^{4046}, \quad R(x) = x - 1,
$$
$$
\text{then } P(x) = Q(x)(x-1) = -1 - x - x^2 - \cdots - x^{2023} + x^{2024} + x^{2025} + \cdots + x^{4047}.
$$
Then $a = 1$ and $b = 2024$, with $b > 2023a$.

**Alternative solution.** Consider the following two polynomials:
$$
P(x) = (x^3 - 1)^N, \quad Q(x) = (x^2 + x + 1)^N.
$$
By the construction of $P(x) : Q(x)$, that is, the polynomial $R(x)$ exists. Since
$$
P(x) = (x^3 - 1)^N = \sum_{j=0}^{N} C_N^j x^{3j} \Rightarrow a = C_N^j \text{ for some } j = 0, N \Rightarrow a = C_N^j < \sum_{j=0}^{N} C_N^j = (1+1)^N = 2^N.
$$
The sum of the coefficients of the polynomial $Q(x)$ is equal to $Q(1) = (1 + 1 + 1)^N = 3^N$ and the number of coefficients is $2N + 1$, because it has degree $2N$. Therefore, according to Dirichlet's principle, there is a coefficient at least
$$
\frac{3^N}{2N + 1} \Rightarrow b \ge \frac{3^N}{2N + 1}.
$$
It is clear that with sufficiently large $N$ inequality will hold:
$$
\frac{b}{a} \ge \frac{3^N}{2^N(2N + 1)} > 2023.
$$
sourceName: MathNet transcription of UKRAINIAN MATHEMATICAL COMPETITIONS
ratingReason: A triangular coefficient profile has bounded first differences but an arbitrarily high peak.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - Second Day - 10th grade
statement:
You are given $n \ge 2$ distinct positive integers. For each pair $a < b$ of these numbers, consider the difference $b - a$. For each of these differences, Vlada writes down the maximum power of two by which this difference is divisible. What is the largest possible number of distinct numbers that Vlada could write?
(Oleksii Masalitin)
solution:
Choose one pair realizing each distinct valuation and draw these pairs as edges on the $n$ numbers. This graph has no cycle. Otherwise, choose the edge of smallest valuation $v$ on a cycle. Every other edge difference is divisible by $2^{v+1}$; adding the signed differences around the rest of the cycle implies that the chosen edge difference is also divisible by $2^{v+1}$, a contradiction. A forest on $n$ vertices has at most $n-1$ edges.
Equality is attained by $1,1+2,1+2^2,\ldots,1+2^{n-1}$: the differences from 1 already realize $n-1$ distinct powers. Thus the answer is $n-1$.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of UKRAINIAN MATHEMATICAL COMPETITIONS
ratingReason: A cycle cannot have pairwise different edge valuations; one edge per valuation must therefore form a forest.
license: MathNet CC BY4.0; original contest rights retained where asserted

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - Second Day - 10th grade
statement:
Consider a complete graph with 4046 vertices with edges colored in some colors. We call a graph $k$-good graph if all the vertices of the graph can be divided into 2023 pairs in such a way that among the colors of the 2023 of the edges connecting the vertices in the pairs are exactly $k$ distinct colors. Is it possible that the graph is 999-good and 1001-good, but not 1000-good?

(Anton Trygub)
solution:
Yes. Divide the vertices into two groups of odd size $2023$. Give every edge between groups one common colour, and give every edge within either group its own private colour. In a perfect matching let $t$ be the number of cross-group edges. The $2023-t$ remaining vertices in each group must be paired internally, so $t$ is odd. Also $t\ge1$. The matching therefore uses
$$1+(2023-t)=2024-t$$
distinct colours, always an odd number. Hence 1000 is impossible. To obtain 999 or 1001 colours, choose respectively $t=1025$ or $t=1023$ cross-group pairs, and pair all remaining vertices within each group. Both constructions are possible because each remaining group size is even.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of UKRAINIAN MATHEMATICAL COMPETITIONS
ratingReason: Colour cross-part edges alike and same-part edges uniquely; the parity of every matching prevents even colour counts.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - First Day - 11th grade
statement: Set $M$ contains $n \ge 2$ positive integers. It is known that for any two distinct numbers $a, b \in M$ the number $a^2 + 1$ is divisible by $b$. Find the largest possible value of $n$.
solution:
**Answer:** $n = 2$.

Suppose that there are at least three numbers in the set $M$, denote them by $a < b < c$. By the condition $b^2 + 1 \vdash c$, and therefore the numbers $b, c$ are mutually prime. Since $a^2 + 1 \vdash b$ and $a^2 + 1 \vdash c \Rightarrow$
$$
a^2 + 1 \vdash bc \ge (a+1)(a+2) = a^2 + 3a + 2.
$$
We obtained a contradiction that proves that $n \le 2$, and for $n = 2$ it is enough to consider, for example, the set $M = \{1, 2\}$.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of UKRAINIAN MATHEMATICAL COMPETITIONS
ratingReason: Three ordered entries would force their two larger, coprime values to divide a²+1, exceeding it.
license: MathNet CC BY4.0; original contest rights retained where asserted

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - First Day - 11th grade
statement: On the plane 2022 points $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_{2022}$ are given, no three of which lie on the same line. Consider all the angles $A_i A_j A_k$ for the triples of distinct points $A_i, A_j, A_k$. What largest number of these angles can be right?
solution:
Consider any point $A_i$ and count the number of pairs of points $(A_j, A_k)$ such that $\angle A_i A_j A_k = 90^\circ$. For each point $A_j$ there exists at most one point $A_k$ (because on the line through $A_j$ perpendicular to $A_iA_j$ there can be at most one point other than $A_j$). Also note that if $X$ is the point at the largest distance from $A_i$ then there can be no point $A_k$ with $\angle A_iXA_k = 90^\circ$, because then we would have $A_iA_k > A_iX$.

Thus, each point can be a vertex of the hypotenuse in at most 2020 right triangles at these points. Since the hypotenuse of each triangle has two vertices, the total number of these triangles does not exceed $\frac{2022 \cdot 2020}{2} = 2022 \cdot 1010$.

This number can be achieved because, for example, we could take 2022 points on a circle so that they are divided into 1011 pairs so that in each pair the points form a circle diameter. Note that for each diameter there will be exactly 2020 points that form a right triangle with it. Then we have at least $1011 \cdot 2020$ different right angles.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of UKRAINIAN MATHEMATICAL COMPETITIONS
ratingReason: Count each hypotenuse endpoint, excluding a farthest point; antipodal circle pairs attain the bound.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - First Day - 11th grade
statement: In quadrilateral $ABCD$, the angles at $B,D$ are right angles. Write $P=AC\cap BD$, $Q=AB\cap CD$, $R=AD\cap BC$. Let $\ell$ be the midline of triangle $PQR$ parallel to $QR$. Prove that the circumcircles of the triangles bounded by $AB,AD,\ell$ and by $CD,CB,\ell$ are tangent.
solution: Let $l$ intersect $AB, AD, BC, CD$ at the points $M, N, K, L$ and let $E = AC \cap QR$. Since $C$ is the orthocenter $AQR$, $AC \perp QR$, and therefore $l$ is the perpendicular bisector of the segment $PE$ (fig. 15). Since $BC$ and $BA$ are the internal and external bisectors of the angle $DBE$, the points $K$ and $M$ are the midpoints of the arcs *PE* of the circumscribed circle of *BPE*. Similarly, the points *L* and *N* are the midpoints of the arcs *PE* of the circumscribed circle of *DPE*. Then $\angle EKL = \angle EBM = \angle ARQ = \angle ECL$, and hence the points *C*, *L*, *K*, *E* lie on the same circle. Similarly, *A*, *M*, *N*, *E* lie on the same circle. It remains to see that $\angle LEM = \angle AEM - \angle CEL = \angle ANM - \angle CKL = \angle ARQ - \angle CRQ = 90^\circ - \angle QAR$. Similarly, $\angle KEN = 90^\circ - \angle QAR = \angle LEM$, so the circumcircles of the triangles *AMN* and *CKL* are in contact.

ratingReason: The proof requires an orthic interpretation, paired angle-bisector constructions and several linked cyclic quadrilaterals.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - First Day - 11th grade
statement:
Find all such functions $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that for any real $x, y$ the following equality holds:
$$
f(x + y f(x + y)) = f(y^2) + x f(y) + f(x).
$$
solution:
**Answer:** $f(x) = x$, $f(x) = 0$.

Let us denote the given equation by (1):
$$
f(x + y f(x + y)) = f(y^2) + x f(y) + f(x). \quad (1)
$$

Substitute $x = y = 0$ into (1):
$$
f(0) = 2f(0) \implies f(0) = 0.
$$

Substitute $x = 0$ into (1):
$$
f(y f(y)) = f(y^2). \quad (2)
$$

Substitute $y = -x$ into (1):
$$
f(x + (-x) f(x - x)) = f(x^2) + x f(-x) + f(x) \implies f(x) = f(x^2) + x f(-x) + f(x)
$$
So,
$$
f(x^2) = -x f(-x). \quad (3)
$$

Now, substitute $x \to -x$ in (3):
$$
f(x^2) = -(-x) f(-(-x)) = x f(x)
$$
So,
$$
f(x^2) = x f(x)
$$
Comparing with (3):
$$
x f(x) = -x f(-x) \implies f(-x) = -f(x). \quad (4)
$$
So $f$ is odd.

Now, substitute $y = -y$ in (1):
$$
f(x + (-y) f(x - y)) = f(y^2) + x f(-y) + f(x)
$$
But $f(-y) = -f(y)$, so
$$
f(x + (-y) f(x - y)) = f(y^2) - x f(y) + f(x)
$$
Let us write this as:
$$
f(x + y f(y - x)) = f(y^2) - x f(y) + f(x). \quad (5)
$$

Now, consider the difference between (1) and (5):
$$
f(x + y f(x + y)) - f(x + y f(y - x)) = 2x f(y). \quad (6)
$$

Suppose that for some $x_0 \neq 0$, $f(x_0) = 0$. Substitute $y = x_0 - x$ into (1):
$$
\begin{align*}
f(x + (x_0 - x) f(x + x_0 - x)) &= f((x_0 - x)^2) + x f(x_0 - x) + f(x) \\
f(x) &= f((x_0 - x)^2) + x f(x_0 - x) + f(x) \\
f((x_0 - x)^2) &= -x f(x_0 - x)
\end{align*}
$$
But from (3):
$$
f((x_0 - x)^2) = -(x_0 - x) f(x - x_0) = (x_0 - x) f(x_0 - x)
$$
So,
$$
-x f(x_0 - x) = (x_0 - x) f(x_0 - x) \implies f(x_0 - x) = 0, \forall x \in \mathbb{R}.
$$
Thus, $f$ is identically zero, $f(x) = 0$ for all $x$.

If $f$ is not identically zero, then such $x_0 \neq 0$ cannot exist. Thus, from the condition $f(x_0) = 0$ it follows that $x_0 = 0$.

Now, let us prove injectivity. Suppose $\exists x_1 \neq x_2$ such that $f(x_1) = f(x_2)$.
In (6), substitute $x = \frac{x_1 - x_2}{2}$, $y = \frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}$:
$$
\begin{align*}
f\left(\frac{x_1 - x_2}{2} + \frac{x_1 + x_2}{2} f(x_1)\right) - f\left(\frac{x_1 - x_2}{2} + \frac{x_1 + x_2}{2} f(x_2)\right) &= (x_1 - x_2) f\left(\frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}\right) \\
(x_1 - x_2) f\left(\frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}\right) &= 0
\end{align*}
$$
So, either $x_1 = x_2$ (contradicts assumption), or $f\left(\frac{x_1 + x_2}{2}\right) = 0$. But as above, the only zero is at $0$, so $x_1 + x_2 = 0 \implies x_1 = -x_2$.
But then
$$
f(x_2) = f(-x_1) = -f(x_1) = -f(x_2) \implies f(x_2) = 0 \implies x_2 = 0 \implies x_1 = 0
$$
So, $f$ is injective.

Now, from (2):
$$
f(y f(y)) = f(y^2)
$$
But $f$ is injective, so $y f(y) = y^2 \implies f(y) = y$ for all $y$.

Thus, the only solutions are $f(x) = 0$ and $f(x) = x$.

It is easy to check that both satisfy the original equation.

ratingReason: Derive oddness and a square identity, then a zero dichotomy and injectivity before concluding.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - Second Day - 11th grade
statement: We call a polynomial *mixed* if it has both positive and negative coefficients (we do not consider zero to be either positive or negative). Is it true that the product of two mixed polynomials is always a mixed polynomial?
solution:
No. Take
$$f(x)=(x^4-x^2+1)(x+1)=x^5+x^4-x^3-x^2+x+1,$$
$$g(x)=(x^2-x+1)(x^2+1)=x^4-x^3+2x^2-x+1.$$
Both have coefficients of both signs. But regrouping their four factors gives
$$f(x)g(x)=[(x^4-x^2+1)(x^2+1)][(x^2-x+1)(x+1)]=(x^6+1)(x^3+1).$$
The product is $x^9+x^6+x^3+1$, with no negative coefficients.
sourceName: MathNet transcription of UKRAINIAN MATHEMATICAL COMPETITIONS
ratingReason: A suitable pair of cyclotomic-style factorizations cancels every negative coefficient.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - Second Day - 11th grade
statement: In triangle $ABC$, $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$ and $K$ the midpoint of $AM$. Choose $X\in AB$, $Y\in AC$ with $AX>BX$, $AY>CY$, $\angle KXM=\angle ACB$ and $\angle KYM=\angle ABC$. Prove that $B,X,C,Y$ are concyclic.
solution:
Let $N$ be the middle of $AB$, and $L$ be the middle of $AC$. Then the points $N$, $K$ and $L$ lie on the same line—the midline of $\triangle ABC$ which is parallel to $BC$ (fig. 19).

Then we have that $\angle KXM = \angle ACB = \angle KNM$, so the quadrilateral $KNXM$ is inscribed, and similarly $KMYL$ is also inscribed.

Therefore, $AN \cdot AX = AK \cdot AM = AL \cdot AY$, so the points $Y$, $N$, $L$ and $X$ lie on the same circle, hence $\angle AXY = \angle ALN = \angle ACB$, so the quadrilateral $BXYC$ is inscribed, which is what we needed to prove.

**Remarks:** In this configuration, the quadrilateral $AXMY$ is harmonic.

ratingReason: Two midpoint circles give a common power from A, which forces the desired cyclicity.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - Second Day - 11th grade
statement:
For a positive integer $n$ we write out all its divisors $1 = d_1 < d_2 < \cdots < d_k = n$. A divisor $d_i$ is called a good divisor if $d_{i-1}d_{i+1}$ is not divisible by $d_i$, $2 \le i \le k-1$. Find all $n$ for which the number of their good divisors is smaller than the number of their different prime divisors.

(Mykhailo Shtandenko)
solution:
**Answer.** $p^\beta$ and $p^\alpha q$, where $q > p^\alpha$ where $p, q$ are prime numbers.

Solution:

First, let's prove that if a number has at least three different prime divisors, it is not suitable for us. Let $m$ be the number of different prime divisors and $p < q$ be the two smallest prime divisors of $n$. Then it is clear that there exists $\alpha$ such that the first consecutive divisors of $n$ will be the numbers $1 < p < p^2 < \cdots < p^\alpha < q$. Note that taking as $d_{i+1}$ all prime divisors of $n$ except for the smallest, we get $m-1$ numbers that satisfy the condition. Indeed, all divisors smaller than a prime number are coprime with that number, so $(d_i, d_{i+1}) = 1$, and since $d_{i-1} < d_i$ we get the conclusion. It remains to find another good number. Let $n : p^{\alpha+1}$. Then the divisor $q$ is a good divisor. Indeed, it cannot be followed by a divisor divisible by $q$, because the smallest of these not yet chosen divisors is $pq$, but $p^{\alpha+1} < pq$. So $p^{\alpha+1}$ is the next composite divisor. Then take the last prime number that comes after $q$ (possibly $q$), after which the next composite number will be $p^{\alpha+1}$. Then it will be the desired $m$-th good number. Now let $n$ be not divisible by $p^{\alpha+1}$. Then the next composite divisor is $pq$. If between $q$ and $pq$ there is at least one prime divisor, then we take the last of them as our $m$-th good number. Otherwise, the divisors $p^\alpha, q, pq$ will be consecutive divisors, and hence $\frac{n}{pq}, \frac{n}{q}, \frac{n}{p^\alpha}$ will be consecutive divisors, but then the divisor $\frac{n}{q}$ will be the desired one, because since $\alpha$ is the degree of occurrence of a prime $p$ in the number $n$, $\frac{n}{p^\alpha}$ is not divisible by $p$, and $\frac{n}{pq}$ is not divisible by $p^\alpha$, but $\frac{n}{q} : p^\alpha$, and $\frac{n}{p^\alpha}$ is divisible by more than one prime divisor of $n$, which means that we have not yet taken it into account, which is what we wanted to prove.

If a number is a power of a prime, then obviously it suits us, because it has no good divisors at all. It remains to consider the case when a number has two different prime divisors, which we denote $p < q$. Then it is clear that there exists $\alpha$ that the first consecutive divisors of $n$ will be the numbers $1 < p < p^2 < \cdots < p^\alpha < q$. The divisor $p^\alpha$ is a good divisor, which means it is the only good divisor of our number. Hence, the next divisor after $q$ is a divisor that is divisible by $q$, but the smallest such divisor not yet used is $pq$, and therefore it comes after $q$. However, $p^{\alpha+1} < pq$, and hence our number $n$ is not divisible by $p^{\alpha+1}$. Then, similarly, the divisors $\frac{n}{pq}, \frac{n}{q}, \frac{n}{p^\alpha}$ will be consecutive divisors, and the divisor $\frac{n}{q}$ will be a good divisor. So, $\frac{n}{q} = p^\alpha$, so $n = p^\alpha q$, and $p^\alpha < q$, and the above answer follows. A simple check shows that both answers do indeed satisfy the condition.

section: Fourth Round, April 2023 - Second Day - 11th grade
statement: Every edge of the complete graph on $2024$ vertices is coloured one of three colours. Determine the largest integer $m$ such that every colouring has a connected monochromatic subgraph on at least $m$ vertices. Equivalently, a traveller may choose one transport type and revisit cities, but each journey must use that type.
solution:
Suppose we have a complete graph with each edge colored in one of three colors. We show that there will always exist a connected component of at least one of the colors of size at least $1012$. First, we show that it is possible to color the edges in such a way that connected components of size more than $1012$ vertices do not exist. Let's label the colors with numbers - 1st, 2nd and 3rd. Let's divide the vertices into groups by $506$ - groups "A", "B", "C" and "D". Let all $1012$ vertices of groups "A" and "B" be connected by edges of color 1, all vertices of group "C" - by color 2, group "D" - by color 3. Between them, all vertices are connected by edges of those colors, as shown in fig. 20. Therefore, groups "A" or "B" form a connected component of size $1012$ of color 1. Groups "A" and "C" are of color 2, groups "B" and "D" are of color 3. Obviously, there is no larger connected component in terms of the number of vertices.

Suppose that there exists a coloring such that the largest connected component contains fewer than $1012$ vertices. Let's consider the coloring that gives the smallest answer to the problem.

Consider the largest connected component of one of the colors. This component, or rather the number of vertices in it, is the answer to the problem. If there are several largest components, choose any of them. Let this component correspond to color 1. Let's denote this component as I. Let this component contain exactly $m$ vertices. Note that not all the edges between the vertices of this component have the color 1. But if we repaint all the edges of this component with color 1, then the answer $m$ in the problem will not change. In this case, there are no vertices of the component I from which an edge of color 1 can come out outside this component I, that is, to a vertex that does not belong to the component I.

Next, consider the largest connected component among all other vertices, II, with color 2 or 3. It includes all the vertices that are connected by color 2, i.e., also those that can be reached through the vertices of the component I. For example, if $A \in$ II, $B \in$ I, and for the vertex $C \notin$ I the following conditions are true: $A(II)\ 2 \leftrightarrow B(I)\ 2 \leftrightarrow C$, then we assume that $C \in$ II, but we do not assume that $B \in$ II. In other words, a vertex cannot belong to two components at the same time (this principle will be maintained in the future). The number of vertices in the component II is denoted by $k$. Now we can repaint all edges in this component into color 2, and, again, the answer $m$ in the problem will not change.

Now let's denote by $X_2$ the group of vertices of the component I that are connected to at least one vertex of the component II by an edge of color 2, let their number be $x_2$. Then all the edges between the vertices $X_2$ and the vertices of component II can be colored in color 2. They still form the connected component of color 2 before this coloring, but since the component of color 1 was chosen first, the total number of vertices $k + x_2 \le m$.

Then all the vertices of the component I that are not included in the group $X_2$, we will combine into the group $X_3$ and denote their number by $x_3$. From these vertices, only edges of color 3 can go to each vertex of component II. But then the vertices of the group $X_3$ and the component II form a connected component of color 3. But then from the vertices of the group $X_3$ there cannot be any edges of color 1 or 3 to vertices that are not included in the components I and II. If there is an edge of color 3, then the connected component of color 3 will be larger than the component II, and this contradicts its construction. Therefore, all vertices that are not included in the components I and II are connected by color 2 (since $X_3$ is not empty). We denote all these vertices as a component III. Similarly, the vertices of the group $X_2$ are connected with III only with edges of color 3. But then the components II and III should be connected only by edges of color 1. That is, they form a connected component of color 1. But we initially chose the largest connected component of color 1, which has $m$ vertices. Therefore, groups II and III groups have no more than $m$ vertices, hence $2m \ge 2024$ and this completes the proof.

statement: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with incentre $I$. On its circumcircle, let $M_{A}$, $M_{B}$ and $M_{C}$ be the midpoints of minor arcs $BC$, $CA$ and $AB$ respectively. Prove that the reflection of $M_{A}$ over the line $IM_{B}$ lies on the circumcircle of the triangle $IM_{B}M_{C}$.
solution:
Let $X$ be the reflection of $M_{A}$ over the line $IM_{B}$. We wish to prove that $X$, $M_{C}$, $I$, $M_{B}$ lie on a circle. By WUM, observe that $A$, $I$, $M_{A}$, $B$, $I$, $M_{B}$ and $C$, $I$, $M_{C}$ are collinear. Therefore, by symmetry, we get
$$
\angle IXM_{B} = \angle IM_{A}M_{B} = \angle AM_{A}M_{B} = \angle ABM_{B}
$$
On the other hand, note that
$$
\angle IM_{C}M_{B} = \angle CM_{C}M_{B} = \angle CBM_{B} = \angle ABM_{B}
$$
Thus, we get $\angle IXM_{B} = \angle ABM_{B} = \angle IM_{C}M_{B}$, so by the converse of the inscribed angle theorem, $X$, $M_{C}$, $I$, $M_{B}$ lie on a circle, as required.

statement: The wizards Albus and Brian are playing a game on a square of side length $2n+1$ metres surrounded by lava. In the centre of the square there sits a toad. In a turn, a wizard chooses a direction parallel to a side of the square and enchants the toad. This will cause the toad to jump $d$ metres in the chosen direction, where $d$ is initially equal to $1$ and increases by $1$ after each jump. The wizard who sends the toad into the lava loses. Albus begins and they take turns. Depending on $n$, determine which wizard has a winning strategy.
solution: Brian wins. Use coordinates centred on the square, whose reachable safe lattice points have both coordinates in $[-n,n]$. Brian replies in the direction opposite to Albus. After $t$ complete pairs of moves the total displacement has length at most $t$, since each pair has net displacement one. For $t\le n$, Brian’s $t$th reply is therefore safe. If play reaches pair $n+1$, Albus must jump $2n+1$, which is impossible inside the square. Thus Brian never loses.

statement:
Let $x$, $y$ and $a_{0}$, $a_{1}$, $a_{2}$, $\ldots$ be integers satisfying $a_{0}=a_{1}=0$ and
$$
a_{n+2}=x \cdot a_{n+1}+y \cdot a_{n}+1
$$
for all integers $n \geq 0$. Let $p$ be any prime number. Show that $\operatorname{gcd}\left(a_{p}, a_{p+1}\right)$ is either equal to $1$ or greater than $\sqrt{p}$.
solution:
Assume that $\operatorname{gcd}\left(a_{p}, a_{p+1}\right) \neq 1$ and let $q$ be a prime dividing $\operatorname{gcd}\left(a_{p}, a_{p+1}\right)$. Considering the sequence $a_{0}, a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots$ modulo $q$, any two consecutive terms still uniquely determine the subsequent term. The fact that
$$
a_{p} \equiv a_{p+1} \equiv a_{0} \equiv a_{1} \equiv 0 \quad(\bmod q)
$$
implies that the sequence is periodic and that $p$ is a period. If $d$ is the minimal period, we must have $d \mid p$, so $d \in\{1, p\}$. If $d=1$, then the sequence is constant modulo $q$ and $1=a_{2} \equiv a_{1}=0(\bmod q)$, a contradiction. Therefore $d=p$, and we cannot find $0 \leq i<j<p$ such that $a_{i} \equiv a_{j}$ and $a_{i+1} \equiv a_{j+1}(\bmod q)$, since otherwise the minimal period would be smaller than $p$. But since there are only $q^{2}$ distinct pairs of residue classes modulo $q$, it follows that $p \leq q^{2}$. Since $p$ is a prime and hence not a square, we conclude that $\sqrt{p}<q \leq \operatorname{gcd}\left(a_{p}, a_{p+1}\right)$.
sourceName: Swiss Mathematical Olympiad — official archive
ratingReason: View consecutive terms modulo a prime divisor as a finite-state cycle; its prime period forces a square-root bound.

statement:
Determine the smallest possible value of the expression
$$
\frac{a b+1}{a+b}+\frac{b c+1}{b+c}+\frac{c a+1}{c+a}
$$
where $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $a+b+c=-1$ and $a b c \leq -3$.
solution:
The minimum is $3$, which is obtained for $(a, b, c) = (1, 1, -3)$ and permutations of this triple.

As $a b c$ is negative, the triple $(a, b, c)$ has either exactly one negative number or three negative numbers. Also, since $|a b c| \geq 3$, at least one of the three numbers has absolute value greater than $1$.

If all of $a, b, c$ were negative, the previous statement would contradict $a+b+c = -1$, hence exactly one of $a, b, c$ is negative.

WLOG let $c$ be the unique negative number. So $a, b > 0 > c$, as the value $0$ isn't possible by $|a b c| \geq 3$. Let $S$ be the given sum of fractions. We then have
$$
\begin{aligned}
S+3 & = \sum_{cyc} \frac{a b+1+a+b}{a+b} = \sum_{cyc} \frac{(a+1)(b+1)}{a+b} = \sum_{cyc} -\frac{(a+1)(b+1)}{c+1} \\
& \geq \sum_{cyc} |a+1| = (a+1)+(b+1)-(c+1) = 2a+2b+2
\end{aligned}
$$
using AM-GM on the three pairs of summands respectively for the inequality. We can do this since $a+1, b+1 > 0$ and $-(c+1) = a+b > 0$, so every summand is positive.

So all we want to do now is show $a+b \geq 2$, to conclude $S \geq 3$. From the two given conditions we have $a b (1+a+b) \geq 3$. If $a+b < 2$, then $a b \leq \left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right)^2 < 1$ and thereby $a b (1+a+b) < 3$. So the implication $a b (1+a+b) \geq 3 \Rightarrow a+b \geq 2$ is indeed true.

statement:
Let $D$ be the set of real numbers excluding $-1$. Find all functions $f: D \rightarrow D$ such that for all $x, y \in D$ satisfying $x \neq 0$ and $y \neq -x$, the equality
$$
(f(f(x)) + y) f\left(\frac{y}{x}\right) + f(f(y)) = x
$$
holds.
solution:
Write $c=f(1)
e-1$. Setting $x=y
e0$ yields $f(f(x))=\alpha x$, where $\alpha=(1-c)/(1+c)$. If $\alpha
otin\{0,1\}$, the allowed input $x=-1/\alpha$ would give the forbidden value $-1$. If $\alpha=0$, then $c=1$ and $f(f(1))=f(1)=1$, a contradiction. Hence $\alpha=1$ and $c=0$. Thus $f(0)=f(f(1))=1$ and $f(f(0))=f(1)=0$, so $f(f(y))=y$ for every $y\in D$. Now $x=1$ gives $(1+y)f(y)+y=1$, whence $f(y)=(1-y)/(1+y)$. This maps $D$ to $D$, is an involution, and satisfies $(x+y)f(y/x)+y=x$ whenever the original equation is defined.

statement: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Kimiko starts with $n$ piles of pebbles each containing a single pebble. She can take an equal number of pebbles from two existing piles and combine the removed pebbles to create a new pile. Determine, in terms of $n$, the smallest number of nonempty piles Kimiko can end up with.
solution:
The answer is one pile when $n$ is a power of two, and two otherwise.

First, any configuration with total $2^k$ can be consolidated. Pair up its odd piles and remove one pebble from each member of each pair, creating piles of size two. All piles are now even; divide their sizes by two and apply induction. Implementing the resulting moves at twice their sizes completes the consolidation.

Write $n=2^k+r$, $0<r<2^k$. We construct a pile of size $r$, after which the remaining total $2^k$ can be consolidated by the lemma. Put $h=2^{k-1}$. If $r=h$, simply form piles of sizes $2^k,r$. If $r<h$, form two piles of size $h$ and remove $h-r$ from both, leaving two piles of size $r$; reserve one. If $r>h$, form piles of sizes $2^k,h$ and remove $2^k-r$ from both, leaving the larger pile of size $r$; reserve it. In both cases there are enough initial pebbles and the removal amount is positive and does not exceed the smaller pile.

Finally let $c>1$ be the odd part of $n$. Initially not all pile sizes are divisible by $c$. This remains true: if after a move every size were divisible by $c$, the new pile $2x$ would give $c\mid x$, so both original sizes would also have been divisible by $c$. A single pile of size $n$ would contradict this invariant.

statement: In a garden, there are 2023 rose bushes planted in a row. Each bush contains either red or blue roses. Vicky is taking a walk and wants to pick some of the flowers. She starts at a bush of her choice, and picks a rose from it to add to her basket. She then continues walking down the row and picks a single flower from each bush she visits. Vicky can skip some bushes, but she cannot skip two adjacent bushes. She can leave the garden at any point. Let $r$ and $b$ be the number of red and blue roses she picked, respectively. Determine the maximal value of $|r-b|$ Vicky can achieve, irrespective of the configuration of bushes.
solution:
The guaranteed value is $507$. Suppose red is the majority colour, with $R\ge1012$ red bushes and $B\le1011$ blue bushes. Visit every red bush, skipping alternate bushes in each intervening blue run. At most $\lfloor B/2\rfloor$ blue roses are required, so $r-b\ge507$.

For sharpness use a blue singleton followed by 1011 alternating pairs $RR,BB,RR,BB,\ldots,RR$. If the walk meets $k$ pairs, each met pair contributes at most two roses and each interior pair at least one. More directly, after removing any unfavourable endpoint bushes, a red-favouring walk begins and ends in red pairs: for $m$ red pairs it meets at least $m-1$ blue pairs, so its score is at most $2m-(m-1)=m+1\le507$. A blue-favouring walk confined to the paired part meets at most 505 blue pairs and scores at most 506. If it also uses the initial singleton, between it and each later blue pair is a red pair, giving at most $1+2m-m\le506$. Thus no walk exceeds 507.

statement:
Let $S$ be a non-empty set of positive integers such that for any $n \in S$, all positive divisors of $2^{n}+1$ are also in $S$. Prove that $S$ contains an integer of the form
$$
\left(p_{1} p_{2} \ldots p_{2023}\right)^{2023}
$$
where $p_{1}, p_{2}, \ldots, p_{2023}$ are distinct prime numbers, all greater than 2023.
solution:
Since $S$ is non-empty, it contains some integer $a$. Since $1 \mid 2^{a}+1$, it follows that $1 \in S$ and thus $2^{1}+1=3 \in S$. We call a pair $(m, n)$ of positive integers $k$-valid if we have $m, n \in S$, $n|m| 2^{n}+1$ and $m / n$ is divisible by $k$ distinct primes. We will show inductively that for every $k \geq 1$ there is a $k$-valid pair.

Lemma. If $(m, n)$ is $k$-valid and $p$ is prime divisor of $m / n$, then $\left(p^{\alpha} m, p^{\alpha} n\right)$ is $k$-valid for all integers $\alpha \geq 0$.

Proof. Using LTE, we have $v_{p}\left(2^{p m}+1\right)=v_{p}\left(2^{n}+1\right)+1$ and hence $p n|p m| 2^{p n}+1$. Also, since $p n \in S$, we have $p m \in S$. Because also $p m / p n=m / n$, it follows that $(p m, p n)$ is $k$-valid. Repeating $\alpha$ times gives the desired result.

For $k=1$, take $(m, n)=(3,1)$. Now assume $(m, n)$ is $k$-valid for some $k \geq 1$ and let $p$ be a prime dividing $m / n$. For any integer $t \geq 1$ we have
$$
0<v_{p}\left(2^{t n}+1\right)=v_{p}\left(2^{n}+1\right)+v_{p}(t)<n+\log _{p}(t)
$$
Thus, the $k$ primes we know to divide $m / n$ make up at most a fraction
$$
\prod_{p} p^{n+\log _{p}(t)}<(m / n)^{n} t^{k}
$$
of $2^{t n}+1$. Using the lemma, we can pick $t$ arbitrarily large such that $(t m, t n)$ is still $k$-valid. It follows that $2^{t n}+1$ is divisible by a prime $q$ that does not already divide $m / n$, hence $(t m q, t n)$ is $k+1$-valid. We conclude the solution by picking a $N$-valid pair $(m, n)$ where $N$ is large enough to ensure $m / n$ is divisible by at least 2023 primes greater than 2023. We then use the lemma to make sure the powers of all these primes are in the prime factorisation of $m$ are at least 2023 .

statement: Let $ABC$ and $AMN$ be two similar, non-overlapping triangles with the same orientation, such that $AB = AC$ and $AM = AN$. Let $O$ be the circumcentre of the triangle $MAB$. Prove that the points $O$, $C$, $N$ and $A$ lie on a circle if and only if the triangle $ABC$ is equilateral.
solution:
Let $O'$ be the circumcentre of triangle $NAC$. Consider the rotation of center $A$ and angle $\angle BAC$: the conditions of the problem imply that it maps $B$ to $C$ and $M$ to $N$. Moreover, because it fixes $A$ we know that it maps $O$ to $O'$, and triangle $AOO'$ is also similar to triangle $ABC$. Then

$O, C, N, A$ on a circle $\Longleftrightarrow O'O = O'A \Longleftrightarrow CB = CA \Longleftrightarrow \triangle ABC$ equilateral, as desired.

statement: Determine all monic polynomials $P(x) = x^{2023} + a_{2022} x^{2022} + \cdots + a_{1} x + a_{0}$ with real coefficients such that $a_{2022} = 0$, $P(1) = 1$, and all roots of $P$ are real and less than $1$.
solution:
Write $P(x) = (x - z_{1})(x - z_{2}) \ldots (x - z_{2023})$, where $z_{1}, \ldots, z_{2023}$ are the roots of $P$. Note that $P(1) = 1$ is equivalent to $(1 - z_{1})(1 - z_{2}) \ldots (1 - z_{2023}) = 1$. Furthermore, by Vieta, $z_{1} + z_{2} + \ldots + z_{2023} = 0$. This gives us the two equations
$$
\begin{aligned}
(1 - z_{1}) + (1 - z_{2}) + \ldots + (1 - z_{2023}) & = 2023 \\
(1 - z_{1}) \cdot (1 - z_{2}) \cdot \ldots \cdot (1 - z_{2023}) & = 1
\end{aligned}
$$
By observing that
$$
\frac{1}{2023} \cdot \sum_{i=1}^{2023} (1 - z_{i}) = \left( \prod_{i=1}^{2023} (1 - z_{i}) \right)^{\frac{1}{2023}}
$$
and using the equality case of AM-GM (which can be applied since $1 - z_{i} > 0$ for all $i$), we deduce that $z_{1} = z_{2} = \ldots = z_{2023} = 0$. Therefore, the only solution is $P(x) = x^{2023}$. This polynomial obviously satisfies the desired properties.

ratingReason: Apply AM-GM to one minus each real root: the sum and product force equality.

statement: Let $G$ be a graph whose vertices are the integers. Assume that any two integers are connected by a finite path in $G$. For two integers $x$ and $y$, we denote by $d(x, y)$ the length of the shortest path from $x$ to $y$, where the length of a path is the number of edges in it. Assume that $d(x, y) \mid x-y$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{Z}$ and define $S(G)=\{d(x, y) \mid x, y \in \mathbb{Z}\}$. Find all possible sets $S(G)$.
solution:
The possible sets are $\{0,1\},\{0,1,2\},\{0,1,2,3\}$ and $\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$.
Since $d$ is defined as a distance, we also have the triangle inequality, stating that
$$
d(x, y) \leq d(x, z)+d(z, y)
$$
for all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{Z}$. Now note that for all $x \in \mathbb{Z}$ we must have $d(x, x+1) \mid 1$ and thus $d(x, x+1)=1$. Iterating this result with the triangle inequality we find that $d(x, y) \leq |x-y|$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{Z}$. If we consider the graph on $\mathbb{Z}$ where $x, y$ are connected if and only if $|x-y|=1$, then we have $d(x, y)=|x-y|$ which satisfies the condition. Excluding this case, we can assume without loss of generality that $d(0, a)<a$ for some positive integer $a$, after shifting $d$ accordingly. Moreover, we can assume that $a$ is the smallest positive integer with this property. If $d(0, a)<a-2$, then we would have
$$
d(0, a-1) \leq d(0, a)+d(a, a-1)<(a-2)+1<a-1
$$
contradicting minimality of $a$. Hence, $a-2 \leq d(0, a)<a$. But we must also have $d(0, a) \mid a$, which together with $d(0, a)<a$ implies that $2 \cdot d(0, a) \leq a$. Putting the two inequalities together we find that $2(a-2) \leq 2 \cdot d(0, a) \leq a$, which is equivalent to $a \leq 4$. In particular, we have
$$
d(0,5) \leq d(0, a)+d(a, 5)<a+(5-a)=5
$$
and hence $d(0,5)=1$. Since for all integers $k$ we have
$$
d(k+1, k+6) \leq d(k+1, k)+d(k, k+5)+d(k+5, k+6)=d(k, k+5)+2
$$
and similarly $d(k, k+5) \leq d(k+1, k+6)+2$, it follows that $d(k, k+5)=1$ for all $k \in \mathbb{Z}$. Now note that for all $k, t$ we have
$$
d(k, t+6) \leq d(k, t)+d(t, t+5)+d(t+5, t+6)=d(k, t)+2
$$
and similarly $d(k, t) \leq d(k, t+6)+2$. It follows by induction that $d(k, k+6 t \pm 1)=1$, where the base case $t=0$ is trivial and we use the fact that $6 t \pm 1$ is coprime to 2 and 3. Now since each integer is at most distance 2 from an integer of the form $6 t \pm 1$, it follows that $d(x, y) \leq 3$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{Z}$.
Now set $S=\{d(x, y) \mid x, y \in \mathbb{Z}\}$ and note that certainly $0,1 \in S$. If $3 \in S$, then we must also have $2 \in S$ since any shortest path of length 3 can be shortened to a shortest path of length 2. The only remaining possibilities for $S$ are
$$
\{0,1\}, \quad\{0,1,2\} \quad \text{and} \quad\{0,1,2,3\}
$$
Now consider the graph where $x$ and $y$ are connected if and only if
$$
x-y \equiv \pm 1 \quad(\bmod 6)
$$
and a quick check shows that this graph satisfies the condition and $S=\{0,1,2,3\}$. Considering instead the graph where $x$ and $y$ are connected if they are of different parity, we also check that the condition is met and $S=\{0,1,2\}$. Finally considering the complete graph on $\mathbb{Z}$ also shows that $S=\{0,1\}$ is possible.
sourceName: Swiss Mathematical Olympiad — official archive
ratingReason: Global propagation of shortcuts and several sharp infinite-graph constructions exceed the target band.

statement:
For a positive integer $m$, we denote by $[m]$ the set $\{1,2, \ldots, m\}$. Let $n$ be a positive integer and let $\mathcal{S}$ be a non-empty collection of subsets of $[n]$. A function $f:[n] \rightarrow [n+1]$ is called kawaii if there exists $A \in \mathcal{S}$ such that for all $B \in \mathcal{S}$ with $A \neq B$ we have
$$
\sum_{a \in A} f(a) > \sum_{b \in B} f(b)
$$
Prove that there are always at least $n^{n}$ kawaii functions, irrespective of $\mathcal{S}$.
solution: For each $g:[n]\to[n]$, choose a set $A\in\mathcal S$ maximizing $\sum_{a\in A}g(a)$ (break ties by any fixed ordering). Define $f(i)=g(i)+1$ for $i\in A$, and $f(i)=g(i)$ otherwise. For $B\ne A$, the difference of its new weight from that of $A$ is governed by $$\sum_A f-\sum_B f=\sum_A g-\sum_B g+|A\setminus B|.$$ This is positive unless $A\subset B$; in that case positivity of $g$ already contradicts the maximizing choice of $A$. Thus $f$ has unique maximizing set $A$. Recover $A$ from $f$, then subtract one on $A$ to recover $g$. This is an injection from the $n^n$ maps $g$ into the required functions.
sourceName: Swiss Mathematical Olympiad — official archive
ratingReason: Raise weights on one maximizing subset; positivity makes the maximum unique and the map invertible.

statement:
Determine all integer values that the expression
$$
\frac{p q + p^{p} + q^{q}}{p + q}
$$
can take, where $p$ and $q$ are both prime numbers.
solution:
Answer: The only possible integer value is $3$.

If both $p$ and $q$ are odd, then the numerator is odd while the denominator is even. Since an even number never divides an odd number, this does not lead to an integer value. Hence we can assume that one of our primes is even and therefore equal to $2$. Since the expression is symmetric in $p$ and $q$, we can assume without loss of generality that $q = 2$.

Substituting $q = 2$, it remains to determine all integer values taken by the expression
$$
\frac{2p + p^{p} + 4}{p + 2} = \frac{2(p + 2) + p^{p}}{p + 2} = 2 + \frac{p^{p}}{p + 2}
$$
In order for this to be an integer, we must have that $p + 2$ is a divisor of $p^{p}$. But since $p$ is prime, the only positive divisors of $p^{p}$ are $1, p, p^{2}, \ldots, p^{p-1}$ and $p^{p}$. If $p > 2$, then we have
$$
p < p + 2 < p + p = 2p < p^{2}
$$
and $p + 2$ is strictly squeezed between two consecutive divisors of $p^{p}$. It follows that for $p > 2$ the expression $p + 2$ never divides $p^{p}$ and we don't get integer values. The only case remaining is $p = q = 2$, making the original expression equal to $3$.
sourceName: Swiss Mathematical Olympiad — official archive
ratingReason: Parity forces a prime to be two, after which a simple divisibility argument gives the only value.
license: MathNet CC BY4.0; original contest rights retained where asserted

statement:
Determine all triples $(a, b, p)$ of positive integers where $p$ is prime and the equation
$$
(a+b)^{p} = p^{a} + p^{b}
$$
is satisfied.
solution:
$(a, b, p) = (1, 1, 2)$ is the only solution. Let's split the problem into two cases.

- Case 1: $a = b$

The equation simplifies into $2^{p} a^{p} = 2 p^{a}$, and since $4 \mid 2^{p}$, $2 \mid p^{a}$ which implies that $p = 2$. Plugging this new piece of information in the initial equation yields $4 a^{2} = 2^{a+1}$ so $a^{2} = 2^{a-1}$. If $a > 1$, then $a$ has to be even since $2^{a-1}$ is even. However, on the other hand, since $a^{2}$ is a perfect square, $2^{a-1}$ has to be a perfect square as well, so $a$ must also be odd, which is a contradiction. Thus, the only option is $a = 1$ which indeed satisfies the initial equation. Thus, out of this case, we obtain one solution: $(a, b, p) = (1, 1, 2)$.

- Case 2: $a \neq b$

Since the equation is symmetric in $a$ and $b$, assume wlog $b > a$. Now, the equation can be rewritten as
$$
(a+b)^{p} = p^{a} (1 + p^{b-a})
$$
Therefore, $p \mid (a+b)^{p}$, so $p \mid a+b$. Now, look at the prime factorisation of both sides of the equation and consider the powers of $p$. The right side of the equation is $p^{a}$ times a number not divisible by $p$, because $b-a > 0$. If $(a+b)^{p} = p^{x} \cdot y$ where $y$ is not divisible by $p$, then $p \mid x$. Thus, we have $p \mid a$, because $x = a$. Combining this with $p \mid a+b$, we deduce that $p \mid a, b$. Now, to conclude, observe that $p^{a}(1 + p^{b-a})$ is a perfect $p$-th power, and since $p^{a}$ is a perfect $p$-th power and is coprime to $1 + p^{b-a}$, we get that $1 + p^{b-a}$ is a $p$-th power. Write $1 + p^{b-a} = z^{p}$, and since $p \mid b-a$ and $b-a > 0$, we get that $z^{p} - p^{b-a} = 1$ which is a contradiction because the difference of 2 different perfect $p$-th powers is at least $2^{p} - 1 > 1$. Thus, in this case, there are no solutions.
sourceName: Swiss Mathematical Olympiad — official archive
ratingReason: Separate equal exponents, then use the p-adic valuation to obtain impossible consecutive positive pth powers.

statement:
during the World Cup, there are $n$ different Panini stickers to collect. Marco's friends are trying to complete their collection, but nobody has a full set of stickers yet! A pair of his friends are said to be wholesome if their combined collection has at least one of each sticker. Marco knows the contents of everyone's collections, and wants to take them all to a restaurant for his birthday. However, he doesn't want any wholesome pairs sitting at the same table.

a. Show that Marco might need to reserve at least $n$ different tables.

b. Show that $n$ tables will always be enough for Marco to achieve his goal.
solution:
to show that at least $n$ different tables are necessary, suppose we had $n$ people, each of which are only missing a sticker, with each person missing a different sticker. Any two of these people are wholesome together, so they must be seated at different tables.

Now, to show that $n$ is always sufficient, simply distribute the friends as follows: associate each type of sticker to a table. The people owning this sticker will not be seated at this table. Make the table instead available to everyone not owning that sticker, and let each person choose whichever table they want to sit in of the options available to them (i.e., the tables corresponding to the stickers they don't own) or just pick it for them. This way, two people who are wholesome cannot be sitting in the same table because if this was the case, they would be missing the same sticker, a contradiction.
sourceName: Swiss Mathematical Olympiad — official archive
ratingReason: Group each collection by a missing sticker type; collections each missing one distinct type give sharpness.

statement: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Roger has a $(2 n+1) \times (2 n+1)$ square garden. He puts down fences to divide his garden into rectangular plots. He wants to end up with exactly two horizontal $k \times 1$ plots and exactly two vertical $1 \times k$ plots for each even integer $k$ between $1$ and $2 n+1$, as well as a single $1 \times 1$ square plot. How many different ways are there for Roger to do this?
solution:
There are $2^n$ tilings. First all rectangle edges have integer coordinates: a horizontal or vertical line avoiding the finitely many edges partitions the side length into integer lengths, so every tile edge it crosses has integer coordinate.

A vertical strip of length $2n$ therefore touches the top or bottom. If it touches neither vertical side, the widths available on either side are less than $2n$, so both horizontal strips of length $2n$ would have to lie in the remaining single row. This is impossible. Thus each of the four longest strips contains a corner. They contain different corners, and the nonoverlap condition forces either the clockwise or the counterclockwise arrangement around the border. Removing them leaves a $(2n-1)\times(2n-1)$ square with precisely the analogous smaller tiles. There are two choices at each of the $n$ stages, and each choice works.
sourceName: Swiss Mathematical Olympiad — official archive
ratingReason: Prove the four longest strips must occupy the corners, giving exactly two orientations per concentric layer.

statement: Triangle $ABC$ satisfies $2\angle CBA=3\angle ACB$. Points $D,E$ on $AC$, in the order $A,D,E,C$, trisect angle $ABC$: $\angle ABD=\angle DBE=\angle EBC$. The bisector of $\angle ACB$ meets $AB$ at $F$. Prove $BE\parallel DF$.
solution: Die Bedingung $2 \cdot \angle CBA = 3 \cdot \angle ACB$ in der Aufgabe bedeutet genau, dass $\angle DCF = \angle FCB = \angle EBD = \angle DBF$ gilt. Aus $\angle DCF = \angle DBF$ können wir folgern, dass $FDCB$ ein Sehnenviereck ist. Daher gilt $\angle FDB = \angle FCB = \angle EBD$, was beweist, dass $BE$ und $DF$ parallel sind.

statement:
Let $JK$ be a diameter of circle $\omega_1$ and $U
e J$ lie on its tangent at $J$. The smaller circle centred at $U$ tangent to $\omega_1$ touches it at $Y$. Let $I
e J$ be the second intersection of $JK$ with $(JYU)$, and $F
e Y$ the second intersection of $KY$ with the circle centred at $U$. Prove that $FUJI$ is a rectangle.
solution: Let $O$ be the centre of $\omega_1$. Tangency gives collinear $U,Y,O$. Since $UF=UY$ and $OY=OK$, angle chasing gives $\angle YFU=\angle UYF=\angle OYK=\angle YKJ=\angle YJU$. Thus $J,Y,U,F$ are concyclic, and $F$ lies on $(JYU)$. Now $UJ\perp JI$ because $UJ$ is tangent at $J$, while $JY\perp YF$ because $JK$ is a diameter. The corresponding angles of the circle $(JYU)$ show that all four angles of $FUJI$ are right angles.
sourceName: Swiss Mathematical Olympiad — official archive
ratingReason: Two isosceles triangles place F on the auxiliary circle; the diameter and tangent then give four right angles.

statement: Positive integers $z_1,\ldots,z_n$ satisfy $z_j\le j$ and have even sum. Prove that signs can be chosen so that $z_1\pm z_2\pm\cdots\pm z_n=0$.
solution: Induct on the list length; the empty list has sum zero. If the last two entries are equal, remove them and apply induction, then give them opposite signs. Otherwise replace them by their positive absolute difference. This is at most $n-1$, and the new total is still even, so induction applies to the resulting list of length $n-1$. Expanding the signed difference gives the required signs for the original two entries. Finally reverse all signs if necessary to make the first sign positive.
sourceName: Austrian Mathematical Olympiad — official final solutions
ratingReason: Induct by replacing the last two entries by their absolute difference; the bounds and parity survive.

statement: A transparent $7\times7$ square grid has some green cells. It may be rotated or reflected, then placed exactly on a $7\times7$ board. Every chosen board cell must be coverable by a green cell in some placement. What is the fewest green cells possible?
solution: Use coordinates $(x,y)\in\{-3,-2,\ldots,3\}^2$ measured from the centre. Rotations and reflections preserve the unordered pair $\{|x|,|y|\}$, and they can map any cell to any other cell with that same pair. There are $\binom{5}{2}=10$ such unordered pairs, allowing repetitions, from $0,1,2,3$. At least one green cell is needed for each pair, and choosing one cell of each type covers every cell under a suitable symmetry. The answer is therefore $10$.
sourceName: DMFA Slovenia — 67th national competition, 22 April 2023
ratingReason: Classify cells under rotations and reflections; each orbit requires one representative and one suffices.

statement: In $ABC$, suppose $AB=AC$ and $\angle A<60^\circ$. Choose $D\in AC$ with $\angle DBC=\angle A$. The perpendicular bisector of $BD$ meets the parallel to $BC$ through $A$ at $E$. Choose $F$ on ray $CA$ beyond $A$ with $AF=2AC$. Prove $BE\parallel AC$, and that the perpendiculars from $F$ to $AB$ and from $E$ to $AC$ meet on $BD$.
solution: Normalize $B=(-1,0)$, $C=(1,0)$, $A=(0,h)$, where $h>\sqrt3$. Similarity of $BCD$ and $ABC$ gives $BD=BC=2$. Writing $D=(t,h(1-t))$ in the circle equation $BD=2$ gives $t=(h^2-3)/(h^2+1)$ (the other root is $C$). Write $E=(e,h)$. The equation $EB^2=ED^2$ simplifies to $2e+(1-t)(1+h^2)=0$, so $e=-2$. Thus $\overrightarrow{BE}=(-1,h)=\overrightarrow{CA}$. Also $F=(-2,3h)$. The two requested perpendiculars are $y-3h=-(x+2)/h$ and $y-h=(x+2)/h$; they meet at $T=(h^2-2,2h)$. Now $\overrightarrow{BT}=(h^2-1,2h)$ is proportional to $\overrightarrow{BD}=\frac{2}{h^2+1}(h^2-1,2h)$, proving the concurrency.

statement: Call $n$ admissible if the edges of the complete graph on $n$ vertices can be coloured so that every edge belongs to exactly one monochromatic triangle. Which of $7,8,9,10,11,12$ are admissible?
solution:
Every edge belongs to a unique monochromatic triangle, so these triangles partition the edges. At a fixed vertex they pair the other vertices; hence $n$ is odd. Counting edges gives $3\mid n(n-1)/2$, eliminating 11 as well as the even values.

For $n=7$, label vertices by the seven nonzero binary triples. For each distinct $x,y$, group the three edges joining $x,y,x+y$, with coordinates added modulo two; assign each such triangle its own colour. Every pair belongs to exactly one of these triangles.

For $n=9$, label vertices by pairs of residues modulo three. The lines of the $3\times3$ affine plane (three horizontal, three vertical, and three in each of the two diagonal directions) are triples. Every pair lies on exactly one line. Give the three edges of each line its own colour. Thus precisely $7$ and $9$ work.

statement: Let $K_n=\{(a_1,\ldots,a_n)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^n:\sum ja_j=n\}$. Write $J(a)=|\{j:a_j=1\}|$. Prove $\sum_{a\in K_n}J(a)=\sum_{a\in K_{n+1}}a_2$.
solution: Work with formal power series and put $P(t)=\prod_{j\ge1}(1-t^j)^{-1}$. Marking a coordinate $a_j=1$ contributes $P(t)t^j(1-t^j)$, since its original factor is replaced by $t^j$. Therefore the generating series of the left side is $$P(t)\sum_{j\ge1}(t^j-t^{2j})=P(t)\frac{t}{1-t^2}.$$ Counting coordinate $a_2$ with multiplicity gives $$P(t)(1-t^2)\sum_{k\ge0}kt^{2k}=P(t)\frac{t^2}{1-t^2}.$$ The second series is $t$ times the first. Comparing coefficients of $t^{n+1}$ proves the identity. Every coefficient involves finitely many terms, so these formal manipulations are valid.

statement: Find $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ satisfying $xf(x+y)+yf(y-x)=f(x^2+y^2)$ for all real $x,y$.
solution: Putting $x=y=0$ gives $f(0)=0$. Setting $y=0$ gives $xf(x)=f(x^2)$, and replacing $x$ by $-x$ proves $f(-x)=-f(x)$. Subtract the original equation from its version with $x,y$ exchanged. Oddness gives $$(x-y)f(x+y)=(x+y)f(x-y).$$ Since $x+y$ and $x-y$ can be any two reals, taking the latter equal to one yields $f(t)=ct$, where $c=f(1)$. Direct substitution verifies every real $c$.

statement: There are 1000 towers, each with 1000 floors and one resident per floor. Each tower uses all 1000 hat colours once. Residents are friends exactly when their hat colours match and their floor numbers differ by one. Find the greatest possible number of unordered friend pairs.
solution: For any fixed colour there are 1000 residents. If $u$ occupy odd floors and $1000-u$ even floors, every friendship joins the two groups. Thus that colour contributes at most $u(1000-u)\le250000$ pairs, for a total at most $250000000$. Attain this by putting colours $1,2,\ldots,1000$ in that floor order in 500 towers, and colours $2,1,4,3,\ldots,1000,999$ in the other 500 towers. For each colour, all 500 residents of the first group are friends with all 500 of the second group. The maximum is $250000000$.

ratingReason: Split each colour by floor parity for the upper bound, then attain it simultaneously with paired floors.

statement: Let $ABC$ be acute and scalene, with orthocentre $H$. The circle centred at $A$ through $H$ meets $(BHC)$ again at $T_a$; define $T_b,T_c$ cyclically. Prove $H,T_a,T_b,T_c$ concyclic.
solution: Let $O$ be the circumcentre and choose vector origin $O$. Write the vertices as $a,b,c$; then $h=a+b+c$, and the circumcentre $S_a$ of $BHC$ has vector $b+c$ (its distances to $B,H,C$ all equal the circumradius). The midpoint $E$ of $OH$ is consequently also the midpoint of $AS_a$. Both $A$ and $S_a$ are equidistant from $H,T_a$, so their line is the perpendicular bisector of $HT_a$; hence $EH=ET_a$. Cyclically $EH=ET_b=ET_c$, proving the result.

ratingReason: The midpoint of OH lies on three perpendicular bisectors obtained from the circle centres.

statement: In a finite simple graph, every nonadjacent pair has exactly two common neighbours, and no four vertices induce exactly five edges. Prove that all vertices have equal degree.
solution: The graph is connected, since nonadjacent vertices have a common neighbour. Fix adjacent $A,B$. For a neighbour $X$ of $A$ not adjacent to $B$ and distinct from $B$, the nonadjacent pair $X,B$ has common neighbours $A$ and a unique $Y$. The edges $AX,AB,BY,YX$ exist and $BX$ does not, so $AY$ cannot exist: it would give exactly five edges on these four vertices. Thus $Y$ is an exclusive neighbour of $B$. Conversely, the two common neighbours of the nonadjacent pair $A,Y$ are precisely $B,X$, recovering $X$ uniquely. This bijects the exclusive neighbours of $A$ and $B$. Their common neighbours and their mutual edge contribute equally, so their degrees agree. Connectivity finishes.
sourceName: Macedonian Mathematical Society — 2023 contest material
ratingReason: For adjacent vertices, uniquely pair their exclusive neighbours using the two-common-neighbours condition.

statement: A function $f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ has $f(A)+f(B)+f(C)=0$ for every unit equilateral triangle $ABC$. Prove $f$ vanishes everywhere.
solution: For two unit equilateral triangles on opposite sides of the same base, subtraction gives equal values at their opposite vertices. Those vertices have distance $\sqrt3$, and every pair at that distance arises in this way. Hence $f(P)=f(Q)$ whenever $PQ=\sqrt3$. If $PQ\le2\sqrt3$, choose a point $R$ at distance $\sqrt3$ from both; then $f(P)=f(R)=f(Q)$. Subdivide an arbitrary segment into pieces of length at most $2\sqrt3$ to see that $f$ is constant. The equilateral-triangle condition says three times that constant is zero.
sourceName: Macedonian Mathematical Society — 2023 contest material
ratingReason: Two equilateral triangles sharing a side imply a fixed-distance invariance; intersecting equal-radius circles makes the function constant.

statement: Let $a_1,\ldots,a_n>0$ and $s=a_1+\cdots+a_n<1$. Prove $$\frac{s}{a_1\cdots a_n}\frac{(1-a_1)\cdots(1-a_n)}{1-s}\ge n^{n+1}.$$
